COMMISSION IMPLEMENTING DECISION
of 23.7.2026
pursuant to Articles 29(1), point (a), 30(1), point (a), and 31(1), point (h), of Regulation
(EU) 2022/1925 of the European Parliament and of the Council on contestable and fair
markets in the digital sector
Case DMA.100193 - Alphabet - Online Search Engine - Google Search - Article 6(5)
(Only the English text is authentic)
THE EUROPEAN COMMISSION,
Having regard to the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union,
Having regard to Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 of the European Parliament and of the Council
of 14 September 2022 on contestable and fair markets in the digital sector and amending
Directives (EU) 2019/1937 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Digital Markets Act), in particular Article
29(1), point (a), and Article 30(1), point (a), and Article 31(1), point (h), thereof,1
After consulting the Digital Markets Advisory Committee,2
Whereas:
1. INTRODUCTION
(1) This Decision, adopted pursuant to Article 29(1), point (a), Article 30(1), point (a),
and Article 31(1), point (h), of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925, is addressed to Alphabet
Inc., together with all the legal entities directly or indirectly controlled by Alphabet
Inc. (hereinafter collectively referred to as “Alphabet”). Alphabet Inc. is a publicly
traded company founded in 2015 through a restructuring of Google Inc. It is
headquartered in Mountain View, California, United States of America. Alphabet is a
global technology company, specialised in internet-related services and products that
include online advertising technologies, search, cloud computing, software and
hardware. The company operates various services in the Union, including the services
listed in the following recital. The legal entity providing these services in the Union is
Google Ireland Ltd, an Alphabet subsidiary established in Ireland.
(2) This Decision finds that Alphabet does not comply with Article 6(5) of Regulation
(EU) 2022/1925 with regard to Alphabet’s online search engine (“OSE”) core
1 Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 September 2022 on
contestable and fair markets in the digital sector and amending Directives (EU) 2019/1937 and (EU)
2020/1828 (Digital Markets Act), OJ L 265, 12.10.2022, p. 1-66.
2 The opinion of the Digital Markets Advisory Committee can be found on the Commission’s Comitology
Register under meeting code CMTD(2026)1229:
https://ec.europa.eu/transparency/comitology-register/screen/committees/C114400/consult?lang=en.

2
platform service (“CPS”) Google Search as it treats more favourably in ranking
Alphabet’s other CPSs and distinct services including Alphabet’s
comparison-shopping services, Alphabet’s flights intermediation service,3 Alphabet’s
trains intermediation service, Alphabet’s lodging intermediation service, Alphabet’s
intermediation service for local places Google Maps, Alphabet’s translation services,
Alphabet’s sports results information services and Alphabet’s gaming services than
similar services of third parties.
(3) This Decision is structured as follows:
● Section 2 summarises the procedure leading to the adoption of this Decision;
● Section 3 sets out the legal framework for the assessment of Alphabet’s
compliance with Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 in relation to
Google Search and assesses Alphabet’s arguments in that respect;
● Section 4 describes the Google Search engine results page (“SERP”) following
transactional queries, applies the legal framework to the Google SERP to
determine Alphabet’s compliance with Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU)
2022/1925 in relation to Google Search and assesses Alphabet’s arguments in
that respect;
● Section 5 describes the Google SERP following content queries, applies the
legal framework to the Google SERP to determine Alphabet’s compliance with
Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 in relation to Google Search and
assesses Alphabet’s arguments in that respect;
● Section 6 rebuts Alphabet’s allegations of procedural shortcomings;
● Section 7 concludes on the duration of the infringement of Article 6(5) of
Regulation (EU) 2022/1925;
● Section 8 identifies the addressees of this Decision;
● Section 9 explains the methodology for setting the fine and the amount of the
fine imposed;
● Section 10 outlines the cease and desist order imposed by this Decision and the
requirement for Alphabet to provide explanations on how it plans to comply
with this Decision;
● Section 11 describes the periodic penalty payments necessary to compel
Alphabet to bring the non-compliance with Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU)
2022/1925 effectively to an end.
2. PROCEDURE
(4) On 5 September 2023, the Commission adopted a decision designating Alphabet as a
gatekeeper pursuant to Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 (the “Alphabet
designation decision”). The Alphabet designation decision lists the following core
3 Throughout this Decision, the use of the words “intermediation” or “intermediation service” does not
mean an “Online intermediation service” (OIS) as defined in Article 2(2) of Regulation (EU)
2022/1925.

3
platform services (“CPSs”) that are provided by Alphabet, and which individually
constitute an important gateway for business users to reach end users: (i) its online
intermediation service (“OIS”) Google Play; (ii) its OIS Google Maps; (iii) its OIS
Google Shopping; (iv) its OSE Google Search; (v) its video-sharing platform service
YouTube; (vi) its operating system Google Android; (vii) its online advertising
services; and (viii) its web browser Google Chrome.4
(5) Pursuant to Article 3(10) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925, Alphabet had to comply, as
of 7 March 2024, with the obligations laid down, among others, in Article 6(5) of
Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 in relation to the CPSs listed in the Alphabet designation
decision, notably in relation to Google Search.
(6) On 7 March 2024, Alphabet submitted to the Commission pursuant to Article 11(1) of
Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 a report describing the measures it has implemented to
ensure compliance with the obligations laid down in Articles 5, 6 and 7 of that
Regulation (the “Alphabet Compliance Report 2024”). The Commission analysed that
report to determine whether the measures implemented by Alphabet ensure and
demonstrate compliance, as of 7 March 2024, with the obligation laid down in Article
6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 in relation to Google Search.
(7) On 25 March 2024, the Commission adopted a decision opening proceedings pursuant
to Article 20(1) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 with a view to the possible adoption of
a decision pursuant to Article 29 of that Regulation in relation to Alphabet’s
compliance with Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 (the “Opening
Decision”).5
(8) In the context of those proceedings, the Commission sent four requests for information
(“RFIs”) to Alphabet (on 6 May 2024, 4 June 2024, 26 June 2024 and 2 August 2024).
Alphabet responded to the RFI of 6 May 2024 on 4, 14 and 24 June 2024, 15 July
2024 and 19 August 2024. Alphabet responded to the RFI of 4 June 2024 on 28 June
2024. Alphabet responded to the RFI of 26 June 2024 on 15 and 26 July 2024.
Alphabet responded to the RFI of 2 August 2024 on 9 September 2024.
(9) On 6 March 2025, Alphabet submitted to the Commission its second annual
compliance report pursuant to Article 11(1) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 (the
“Alphabet Compliance Report 2025”). In this report, Alphabet maintains that the
measures it had already put in place by 7 March 2024, as detailed in the Alphabet
Compliance Report 2024, comply with Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925.6
Alphabet's Compliance Report 2025 confirms that it has not made any further changes
to these measures.7
(10) On 19 March 2025, the Commission communicated to Alphabet its preliminary
findings pursuant to Article 29(3) and 34(1) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 in the
context of the proceedings referred to in recital (7) of this Decision (the ‘Preliminary
Findings’). In the Preliminary Findings, the Commission reached the preliminary
conclusion that Alphabet failed to comply with the requirements laid down in Article
4 Decision C(2023) 6101 final.
5 Decision C(2024) 2053 final.
6 Alphabet Compliance Report 2025 – Google Search Chapter, paragraph 24, [Attachment ID].
7 Alphabet Compliance Report 2025 – Google Search Chapter, paragraph 54, [Attachment ID].

4
6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925. According to the Commission’s preliminary view,
Alphabet favourably ranks services on Google Search that are distinct from or
additional to Google Search, including, in particular, Alphabet’s comparison-shopping
services, its flights intermediation service, trains intermediation service, lodging
intermediation service, intermediation service for local places, Google Maps,
translation services, sports results information services and gaming services. In the
Commission’s preliminary view, the measures implemented by Alphabet to ensure
compliance did not provide equal prominence to similar services of third parties.8
(11) On 20 March 2025, Alphabet’s specified external advisers requested, on behalf of
Alphabet, access to the Commission’s file pursuant to Article 34(4) of Regulation
(EU) 2022/1925 and Article 8 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU)
2023/814.9 In particular, Alphabet’s specified external advisers requested access to the
non-confidential version of the documents referenced in the Preliminary Findings in
accordance with Article 8(2) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/814, as well as
full access to all documents contained in the Commission’s file without redactions in
accordance with Article 8(3) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/814.10
(12) By the same submission, Alphabet’s specified external advisers sent a letter to the
Commission relating to Alphabet’s access to the file.11 In that letter, Alphabet’s
specified external advisers raised a number of concerns related to access to the file
which allegedly compromised Alphabet’s rights of defence and made additional
requests. These requests were reiterated and supplemented by additional submissions
on 21 March 2025 and 25 March 2025.12 The Commission replied to Alphabet’s
requests by emails of 26 March 2025, 28 March 2025 and 2 April 2025,13 and rejected
some of Alphabet’s claims. As far as Alphabet maintained its claims in response to the
Preliminary Findings, these are discussed in Section 6 of this Decision.
(13) On 21 March 2025, the Commission provided Alphabet and Alphabet’s specified
external advisers, with non-confidential versions of all documents referenced and
relied upon in the Preliminary Findings, pursuant to Article 8(2) of Implementing
Regulation (EU) 2023/814.
(14) In application of Article 8(3) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/814, Alphabet’s
specified external advisers were granted access to the Commission’s file at the
Commission’s premises via a data room between 24 March 2025 and 8 April 2025
pursuant to the Terms of Disclosure laid down in the Commission decision of 21
March 2025 (the ‘Terms of Disclosure Decision’).14 Pursuant to the Terms of
Disclosure Decision, Alphabet’s specified external advisers were granted access to all
documents in the case file with the exception (under Article 8(4) of Implementing

5
Regulation (EU) 2023/814) of correspondence with the United Kingdom’s
Competition and Markets Authority (“CMA”), consisting of minutes of the meetings
between the Commission and the CMA of 17 October 2024 and 16 December 2024
and email exchanges of 29 November 2024 and 10 December 2024 related to the latter
meeting, and correspondence with the United States Department of Justice (“DOJ”),
consisting of minutes of the meeting with the DOJ of 4 December 2024. On 8 April
2025, the data room report was finalised and a non-confidential version of it was
shared with Alphabet.
(15) On 18 May 2025, Alphabet responded to the Preliminary Findings contesting the
Commission’s preliminary conclusions on non-compliance.15
(16) On 6 March 2026, Alphabet submitted to the Commission its third annual compliance
report pursuant to Article 11(1) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 (the “Alphabet
Compliance Report 2026”). Alphabet's Compliance Report 2026 confirms that it has
not made any further changes to the measures it had put in place by 7 March 2024.16
3. LEGAL FRAMEWORK FOR THE ASSESSMENT OF COMPLIANCE WITH ARTICLE 6(5) OF
REGULATION (EU) 2022/1925
(17) Pursuant to Article 29(1), point (a), of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925, where the
Commission finds that a gatekeeper does not comply with any of the obligations laid
down in Articles 5, 6, or 7 of that Regulation, it shall adopt an implementing act
setting out its finding of non-compliance (the “non-compliance decision”). In such a
non-compliance decision, the Commission shall, pursuant to Article 29(5) of
Regulation (EU) 2022/1925, order the gatekeeper to cease and desist with the
non-compliance and to provide explanations on how it plans to comply with that
decision. The Commission may also impose a fine pursuant to Article 30(1), point (a),
of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925, and impose periodic penalty payments pursuant to
Article 31(1), point (h), of that Regulation, to compel a gatekeeper to comply with
such a non-compliance decision.
(18) Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 states that a gatekeeper “shall not treat
more favourably, in ranking and related indexing and crawling, services and products
offered by the gatekeeper itself than similar services or products of a third party”, and
“shall apply transparent, fair and non-discriminatory conditions to such ranking”.
(19) Pursuant to Article 8(1) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925, the measures implemented by
the gatekeeper to ensure compliance with Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925
must be effective in achieving the objectives of that Regulation and of such obligation.
(20) Recital 51 of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 explains that “Gatekeepers are often
vertically integrated and offer certain products or services to end users through their
own core platform services, or through a business user over which they exercise
control which frequently leads to conflicts of interest. This can include the situation
whereby a gatekeeper provides its own online intermediation services through an
online search engine. When offering those products or services on the core platform
service, gatekeepers can reserve a better position, in terms of ranking, and related
15 Alphabet’s response to the Preliminary Findings, submitted on 16 May 2025, [Attachment ID].
16 Alphabet Compliance Report 2026 – Google Search Chapter, paragraph 54, [Attachment ID].

6
indexing and crawling, for their own offering than that of the products or services of
third parties also operating on that core platform service. This can occur for instance
with products or services, including other core platform services, which are ranked in
the results communicated by online search engines, or which are partly or entirely
embedded in online search engines results, groups of results specialised in a certain
topic, displayed along with the results of an online search engine, which are
considered or used by certain end users as a service distinct or additional to the
online search engine. (…)”.
(21) Recital 52 of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 further adds that “In such situations, the
gatekeeper should not engage in any form of differentiated or preferential treatment in
ranking on the core platform service, and related indexing and crawling, whether
through legal, commercial or technical means, in favour of products or services it
offers itself or through a business user which it controls. To ensure that this obligation
is effective, the conditions that apply to such ranking should also be generally fair and
transparent. Ranking should in this context cover all forms of relative prominence,
including display, rating, linking or voice results and should also include instances
where a core platform service presents or communicates only one result to the end
user. To ensure that this obligation is effective and cannot be circumvented, it should
also apply to any measure that has an equivalent effect to the differentiated or
preferential treatment in ranking. The guidelines adopted pursuant to Article 5 of
Regulation (EU) 2019/1150 should also facilitate the implementation and enforcement
of this obligation”.
(22) Article 2, point (6), of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 defines OSEs by reference to
Article 2, point (5), of Regulation (EU) 2019/1150.17 The latter provision defines
OSEs as “a digital service that allows users to input queries in order to perform
searches of, in principle, all websites, or all websites in a particular language, on the
basis of a query on any subject in the form of a keyword, voice request, phrase or
other input, and returns results in any format in which information related to the
requested content can be found”.
(23) Article 2, point (23), of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 further defines ‘search results’ as
“any information in any format, including textual, graphic, vocal or other outputs,
returned in response to, and related to, a search query, irrespective of whether the
information returned is a paid or an unpaid result, a direct answer or any product,
service or information offered in connection with the organic results, or displayed
along with or partly or entirely embedded in them”.
(24) Moreover, Article 2, point (22), of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 defines ‘ranking’ as
“the relative prominence given to goods or services offered through online
intermediation services, online social networking services, video-sharing platform
services or virtual assistants, or the relevance given to search results by online search
engines, as presented, organised or communicated by the undertakings providing
online intermediation services, online social networking services, video-sharing
platform services, virtual assistants or online search engines, irrespective of the
17 Regulation (EU) 2019/1150 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 June 2019 on
promoting fairness and transparency for business users of online intermediation services, OJ L 186,
11.7.2019, p. 57-79.

7
technological means used for such presentation, organisation or communication and
irrespective of whether only one result is presented or communicated”.
(25) In that context, it follows from Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 and recital
51 of that Regulation, that Alphabet should not treat its own distinct or additional
services on its SERP more favourably in ranking as compared to similar services of
third parties that are also ranked on the SERP.
(26) This means that Alphabet does not comply with Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU)
2022/1925 in cases where: (i) Alphabet offers a service that is distinct or additional to
Google Search, and which is ranked on, embedded in, or displayed along search
results communicated by that OSE; (ii) third parties offer similar services to
Alphabet’s distinct or additional service and such third parties’ services are also
ranked on, embedded in, or displayed along search results shown on the SERP; and
(iii) Alphabet treats its own distinct or additional service more favourably in ranking
or related indexing and crawling than those similar services offered by third parties.
3.1. The existence of distinct or additional services to an online search engine that
are ranked on the SERP
3.1.1. The Commission’s position
(27) In the Alphabet designation decision, which Alphabet has not appealed, the
Commission found that all results or outputs that the OSE Google Search shows on its
SERP, regardless of their format or type and irrespective of the means through which
users access such results or the type of device they use, constitute search results within
the meaning of Article 2, point (23), of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925. Such a finding
does not preclude, however, that such search results contain and rank services which
are distinct or additional to an OSE.18
(28) To determine whether Alphabet offers a service that is distinct or additional to Google
Search, and which is ranked in, embedded in, or displayed alongside the search results
of Google Search, it is necessary, as clarified in recital 51 of Regulation (EU)
2022/1925, to examine whether such a service is considered or used by certain end
users as a service distinct or additional to an OSE. As is apparent from Section D(2) of
the Annex to the DMA, examining whether a given service is used by end users or
business users as a service distinct or additional to an OSE requires an assessment of
the service’s purpose, as compared to the purpose of an OSE. Such an assessment
must be carried out by reference to the objective functionalities and tasks performed
by the service in question.
(29) In carrying out this assessment, it is important to take into account that the purpose of
an OSE is set out in Article 2, point (5), of Regulation (EU) 2019/1150, which is
referred to in Article 2, point (6), of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925. These provisions
indicate that the purpose of an OSE is, in essence, to search the Internet and deliver to
users results in which information related to the requested content can be found.19
18 Decision C(2023) 6101 final, recitals 94, 95.
19 The Impact Assessment of the proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council
on promoting fairness and transparency for business users of online intermediation services, SWD
(2018) 138 final, p. 69, sec. 7.2.5, states that “Internet search engines are services that help Internet
users find the relevant answers to their search requests from among tens of billions of web pages on the

8
(30) If, following the above-mentioned assessment, it is concluded that a service which is
ranked in, embedded in, or displayed alongside the search results of Google Search
has a purpose that is different from or goes beyond the purpose of an OSE, that service
is to be considered a distinct or additional service to Google Search.
(31) Recital 51 of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 clarifies that distinct or additional services
to an OSE may take the form of products or services which are ranked in the results
communicated by OSEs, or which are partly or entirely embedded in OSEs results,
groups of results specialised in a certain topic, displayed along with the results of an
OSE.
(32) In light of the above, it must be noted that Alphabet shows distinct or additional
services on the SERP of Google Search, in response to transactional and to
content-related20 search queries, when a given group of results or dedicated unit
specialised in a certain topic has a different purpose to that of an OSE, insofar as it has
functionalities or performs tasks that are different to or go beyond searching the
Internet and delivering to users results in which information related to the requested
content can be found.
(33) As regards transactional queries, this is the case, in particular, when a given group of
results or dedicated unit, specialised in a certain topic, presents a series of
functionalities or performs tasks that, individually or in combination, allow users to
filter, interact with, and compare competing offers, based on relevant commercial
parameters, directly on the SERP, in order to facilitate the initiation of transactions
between businesses and consumers.
(34) As regards content-related queries, this is the case, in particular, when a given group
of results or dedicated unit, specialised in a certain topic, presents a series of
functionalities or performs tasks that, individually or in combination, allow users to
perform, directly on the SERP, actions that are unrelated to or otherwise go beyond
searching the Internet and obtaining results in which information related to the
requested content can be found (e.g., playing a game or translating words or groups of
words from one language to another).
(35) Additionally, it must be noted that services provided by Alphabet that fall into a
category of CPS pursuant to Article 2, point (2), of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 other
than OSE, such as OISs, by definition, have a purpose that is different to that of an
OSE, and therefore are distinct from or additional to Google Search. This is clearly the
case, for instance, for those CPSs – other than Google Search – which the Commission
internet. They facilitate direct interaction between internet users seeking information, website operators
seeking an audience for their content, and online advertisers targeting potential customers. The
fundamental purpose of a search engine is to make it easier for users to find information on the internet.
Given the fact that the number of web pages is constantly increasing (approximately 46 billion indexed
and searchable pages in March 2016) and that the random assignment of web addresses (URLs) does
not provide any practical way of identifying their contents, a search for information would be
impossible without technical assistance”.
20 ‘Transactional’ search queries are queries that relate to purchasing, booking, or otherwise advance
commercial transactions with respect to products or services (for example, goods, flights, trains, hotels,
restaurants or services provided in other physical locations). ‘Content-related’ search queries are queries
aimed at accessing content related to specific categories of information or other services (for example,
translation, sport information or games).

9
listed in the Alphabet designation decision, and which are ranked in, embedded in, or
displayed along search results communicated by Google Search.
(36) Finally, a distinct or additional service to an OSE can also be shown when, regardless
of its purpose, a given group of results or dedicated unit specialised in a certain topic
is not assembled by performing searches of, in principle, all websites, or all websites
in a particular language, as required by the definition of an OSE contained in Article 2,
point (6), of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925, by reference to Article 2, point (5), of
Regulation (EU) 2019/1150. Indeed, in such a case, such a group of results or
dedicated unit does not meet the definition of an OSE, as established in the
abovementioned legal provisions. Consequently, such a group of results or dedicated
unit is, by definition, a distinct or an additional service to an OSE.
(37) This is the case, for instance, when, in response to a transactional or content-related
query, a given group of results or dedicated unit specialised in a certain topic, rather
than showing results obtained by searching in principle all websites, shows results that
have been sourced only or predominantly through means other than searching in
principle all websites (e.g., they are exclusively or predominantly sourced through
licensed data, through data feeds,21 or through data obtained from distinct or additional
services of the gatekeeper), or shows only results obtained from a limited data source
or pool of websites pre-defined or selected by Alphabet.
3.1.2. Alphabet’s arguments
(38) First, Alphabet notes that the output of an OSE includes search results responding to
queries on any subject, presented in any format and with any information.22
(39) In the first place, Alphabet argues that OSEs are not limited to returning results for or
links to websites. Relying on the wording of Article 2, point (23), of Regulation (EU)
2022/1925 and Article 2, point (5), of Regulation (EU) 2019/1150, Alphabet
highlights that the output of an OSE may include search results in any format,
including direct answers, and that the legislator deliberately chose to define the output
of an OSE broadly.23 According to Alphabet, the reference in Article 2, point (5), of
Regulation (EU) 2019/1150 to searching “in principle, all websites” is not a limitation
on the results a search engine can return, but a minimum criterion that an OSE must
meet to qualify as such. To be an OSE, a service must be capable of enabling users to
search for, in principle, all websites. However, an OSE may return results that are not
21 Data feeds are a mechanism to continuously provide real-time information. Specifically, data providers
can, either manually or programmatically via an API (application programming interface) send a
continuous stream of data on pre-defined parameters, such as certain characteristics of products and
services, availability, pricing. Data feeds are used mostly for the provision of information that is volatile
over time because they allow keeping information reliable and up-to-date without any lags. See:
Alphabet’s response to RFI PO 1 of 6 May 2024, submitted on 14 June 2024, paragraph 42,
[Attachment ID] and Alphabet’s response to RFI PO 3 of 26 June 2024, Tranche 1, submitted on 15
July 2024, paragraph 41, [Attachment ID].
22 Alphabet’s response to the Preliminary Findings, submitted on 16 May 2025, paragraphs 34-52,
[Attachment ID].
23 Alphabet’s response to the Preliminary Findings, submitted on 16 May 2025, paragraphs 36-37,
[Attachment ID].

10
websites at all, including direct answers or results for things that exist in the real
world.24
(40) In the second place, Alphabet argues that OSEs do not show results for all websites for
any given query. When a user inserts a query on a specific topic, an OSE only returns
results for the particular type of website relevant to that query.25
(41) In the third place, Alphabet argues that OSEs and OISs overlap. Indeed, OSEs return
results for queries on any subject and enable searches of in principle all websites. The
fact that a particular type of search result might also be returned by an OIS does not
mean that the search result is not part of an OSE.26
(42) In the fourth place, Alphabet submits that OSEs facilitate transactions by
intermediating between users and suppliers. In this regard, Alphabet refers to recital 6
of Regulation (EU) 2019/1150, which, according to Alphabet, recognises that
facilitating transactions is part of what an OSE does.27
(43) In the fifth place, Alphabet argues that OSEs may display results in any format and
with any information. Limiting their ability to do so would hinder their ability to
provide useful and effective results in response to user queries. OSEs organise their
results in different ways in order to respond to different types of queries in the most
effective and helpful way possible.28
(44) In the sixth place, Alphabet argues that OSEs enable users to compare results.
Following a query, OSEs provide users with multiple different results, which users can
then compare in order to select the one that is of particular interest to them. The way
results are formatted and the information they provide help users to compare and
select results.29
(45) Second, Alphabet notes that the inputs of an OSE include the queries that users issue
and the data for its results that it collects via multiple different means.30
(46) In the first place, regarding user queries, Alphabet refers to Article 2, point (5), of

various mechanisms beyond keyword input, including query suggestions and shortcut
chips. This is, in Alphabet’s view, consistent with Regulation (EU) 2019/1150’s
recognition that an OSE can provide different means for users to input queries.31

3.1.3. The Commission’s assessment of Alphabet’s arguments
(50) First, as regards the output of an OSE, the Commission, in the first place,
acknowledges the fact that such output may include not only search results in the form
of links to websites, but also search results in any other format, including direct
answers, as established in Article 2, point (23), of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 and
Article 2, point (5), of Regulation (EU) 2019/1150. Indeed, it is true that search results
may be presented “in any format”. However, it is also true that, irrespective of their
format, search results may contain and rank services which are distinct or additional to
an OSE, as set out in recitals (32) to (37) of this Decision. This is the case, in
particular, if a given group of results or dedicated unit specialised in a certain topic has
specific functionalities or performs tasks that are different to or go beyond searching
the Internet and delivering to users results in which information related to the
requested content can be found, or is not assembled by performing searches of, in
principle, all websites, or all websites in a particular language, as required by the
definition of an OSE.
(51) The Commission notes, additionally, that pursuant to Article 2, point (5), of
Regulation (EU) 2019/1150, an OSE is a service that allows users to “perform
searches of, in principle, all websites, or all websites in a particular language”. The
Commission agrees with Alphabet that this sets out a minimum criterion that a service
must meet in order to qualify as an OSE, in the sense that, if a service does not enable
users to perform searches of, in principle, all websites, or all websites in a particular

searches of, in principle, all websites, or all websites in a particular language, but
instead, for instance, shows only results that have not been sourced from websites at
all or that have been obtained from a limited data source or pool of websites
pre-defined or selected by the provider of the OSE, such a group of results or
dedicated unit can constitute a distinct or additional service to an OSE.
(52) In the second place, the Commission acknowledges the fact, put forward by Alphabet,
that, when a user inserts a query on a specific topic, an OSE will only return a subset
of results for websites that are most relevant to that query, and does not provide the list
and relative ranking (based on the match with the query) of all websites indexed.
Alphabet, however, conflates the mechanism for the retrieval of search results with the
set of information shown to users. Indeed, as stated in recital (29) of this Decision, the
reference contained in Article 2, point (5), of Regulation (EU) 2019/1150 according to
which an OSE must allow users to “perform searches of, in principle, all websites, or
all websites in a particular language” describes a characteristic of an OSE, namely
that of returning a list of results that contain content related to the user’s query and
that are retrieved from a very broad range of sources (i.e., in principle all websites).
This does not however mean that, for each user query, an OSE must return the list of
all websites ranked based on their relevance in relation to the query.
(53) Additionally, Alphabet notes that, if a user searches for a specific topic (e.g., a recipe),
an OSE will return results for websites that provide information on that specific topic
(e.g., recipes), and not websites relating to other topics (e.g., physics). It is true that
returning results sourced from, in principle all websites, limited only to the extent they
have some relationship to each user query, is consistent with the definition of an OSE,
whether it ranks simple blue links or specialised units. However, limiting results to
those that have relevance for the query is not what the Commission refers to when
describing situations where elements on the SERP are not assembled based on a search
of ‘in principle, all websites’, as set out in recitals (36) - (37) of this Decision.
Specifically, whereas, e.g., the simple blue links shown by Google Search on the
SERP can refer users to all types of websites that provide information that is relevant
and specific to the topic of each user query, there are elements ranked on Google
Search which contain information that is systematically not sourced from ‘in
principle, all websites’. For example, showing users who enter a query indicating they
want to buy products results that are relevant for that purpose can be consistent with
the definition of an OSE. On the other hand displaying a dedicated unit which, for
example, for purposes of enabling comparison of product offers systematically shows
only shopping results that are sourced from a specific pool of shopping-related
websites does not show results from in principle, all websites, in particular when the
websites participating in these units are pre-defined or selected by Alphabet on the
basis of specific eligibility criteria selecting only shopping-related businesses that
share specific data or display pre-defined website elements. Those units do therefore
not meet the definition of an OSE.
(54) In the third place, contrary to Alphabet’s assertion, the Commission does not claim
that the distinct or additional services identified in this Decision, except Google Maps
which was designated as such, are OISs. Nevertheless, the Commission does not

13
exclude that, in practice, a partial overlap may exist between OSEs and OISs or any
other distinct or additional services. However, the assessment whether a particular
service may be qualified as an OSE, as an OIS, or as any other type of distinct or
additional service, must be carried out, in particular, in light of the purpose of such
services, as defined in Regulation (EU) 2022/1925.
(55) Moreover, in Article 2, points (2), (5) and (6), of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925, the
legislator drew a clear legal distinction between the notion of an OSE and that of an
OIS. The Impact Assessment of Regulation (EU) 2019/1150 also clearly points to a
distinction between OSEs and other online platforms insofar as it stresses that “Online
platforms and online general search engines are distinct types of online services, with
the latter indexing websites without necessarily entering into contractual relations
with the website users. Online search engines also generate revenue from advertising
rather than from intermediating B2C transactions and they necessarily have to index
the entire Internet in order to provide a quality service (i.e. there is no room for
specialisation in general search)”36. Even if both OSEs and OISs allow users to enter
queries and show results consistent with that query, an important distinction exists
between the purpose of an OSE, which is to search the Internet and deliver to users
results in which information related to the requested content can be found, and the
specialised nature of OISs, which allow users to initiate transactions for a particular
type of product or service. For example, a service specialised in intermediating a
specific type of transaction will, like an OSE, show different results in response to a
user query to the extent that query relates to the type of transaction it specialises in.
However, differently from an OSE, such a service will not use as sources all websites,
but only those that are related to queries in the category of transactions it
intermediates.
(56) In the fourth place, it is true that, according to recital 6 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1150,
at least in some cases, an OSE may incidentally facilitate a transaction. However, it is
clear in particular from recital 10, Article 2, point (2)(b), and Article 2, point (5), of
that Regulation that, while facilitating the initiation of direct transactions between
business users and consumers is a constitutive part of the purpose of an OIS, this is not
a part of the purpose of an OSE. This means that, if the purpose of a given digital
service is to facilitate the initiation of transactions, such a service is more
appropriately qualified as an OIS than it is as an OSE. Indeed, while OSEs may, in
response to a transactional query, refer users to commercial websites, for the same
given query they may also show many different kinds of results, from all websites that
are relevant to that query. Conversely, showing results only from a pre-defined and
limited type of businesses that offer a specific type of transactional offers, together
with functionalities enabling users to filter, interact with, and compare search results
for that type of offers facilitates the initiation of transactions. This is different from, or
at least goes beyond the purpose of an OSE. The broad interpretation put forward by
Alphabet, according to which, in essence, facilitating transactions would also be the
purpose of an OSE, would render the legal distinction between OSEs and OISs
meaningless.

(57) In the fifth place, the Commission acknowledges the fact that OSEs may display
results in any format and with any information, as established in Article 2, point (23),
of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 and Article 2, point (5), of Regulation (EU) 2019/1150.
The fact remains, however, as also explained in recital (27) of this Decision, that such
search results may contain and rank services which are distinct or additional to an
OSE.
(58) In the sixth place, as regards Alphabet’s argument that OSEs enable users to compare
search results, it is important to make a distinction between, on the one hand, enabling
users to choose among search results depending on their relevance to a user query,
and, on the other, enabling users to select products or services directly on the SERP,
among products or services specialised in a certain topic, based on relevant
commercial parameters by filtering, interacting with, and comparing transactional
offers on the SERP, with a view to initiating a transaction. While the first action relates
to searching the Internet and obtaining results in which information related to the
requested content can be found, and falls within the purpose of an OSE, the second
one relates to transactional intermediation and goes beyond the purpose of an OSE.
(59) Second, as regards the inputs of an OSE, the Commission, in the first place,
acknowledges the fact that, pursuant to Article 2, point (5), of Regulation (EU)
2019/1150, an OSE may allow users to issue queries through various mechanisms,
including for instance query suggestions and shortcut chips. Thus, the fact that a
specific query mechanism is available to users is not in itself determinative of a
service going beyond the purpose of an OSE. However, if, for instance, a query
mechanism such as a query shortcut chip, in combination with other functionalities,
enables users to filter, interact with, and compare competing transactional offers,
based on relevant commercial parameters, directly on the SERP, in order to facilitate
the initiation of a transaction, the existence of that query mechanism will contribute
towards the conclusion that there is a service which is distinct or additional to an OSE.
(60) In the second place, as regards Alphabet’s argument that using multiple different
means to collect data (including not only crawling but also, for instance, licensed
sources, data feeds, and direct uploads) is consistent with the purpose of an OSE, the
Commission notes that, as explained in recital (37) of this Decision, when in response
to a given query Google Search returns a group of results, or dedicated unit,
specialised in a certain topic, which is sourced only or predominantly through means
other than searching in principle all websites, such a group of results or dedicated unit
are, by definition, a distinct or additional service. The fact that certain groups of
results or dedicated units displayed by Alphabet on the SERP show only results
obtained from a limited data source or pool of websites pre-defined or selected by
Alphabet is evidence of the presence of an additional or distinct service.
(61) Third, the Commission agrees with Alphabet that, pursuant to Section D(2) of the
Annex to Regulation (EU) 2022/1925, to determine whether a service is distinct or
additional to an OSE, it should be established, in particular, whether such a service has
a different purpose from that of an OSE (see recital (27) of this Decision). The
Commission is of the view that such an assessment should be carried out objectively
by reference to the specific functionalities or tasks that the service in question
performs rather than relying on subjective user perceptions or expectations as

15
Alphabet claims.37 Alphabet correctly points out that the Commission’s assessment is
not, and should in the Commission’s view not be, based on evidence regarding user
expectations, perceptions or behaviour.38
(62) In the first place, Article 2, point (5), of Regulation (EU) 2019/1150, which is referred
to in Article 2, point (6), of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925, defines an OSE and clearly
sets out the purpose and characteristics of such a service. The functionalities and tasks
set out in this provision determine the purpose for which an OSE is intended to be
used and can therefore be assumed to be used. If a given service is used, in view of the
specific functionalities and tasks that it performs, for a purpose that is different to or
goes beyond searching the Internet and delivering to users results in which
information related to the requested content can be found, it should be concluded that
such a service has a different purpose to that of an OSE and qualifies as a distinct or
additional service under Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925.
(63) In the second place, pursuant to Article 1(1) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925, that
Regulation is meant to contribute to the proper functioning of the internal market by
laying down harmonised rules. The application of harmonised rules would be impaired
if the assessment of a distinct or additional service depended on user perceptions or
expectations, which as these are subjective and may vary by user groups.
(64) In the third place, user perceptions or expectations are driven by the design of Google
Search as the major OSE in the Union. User expectations, perceptions, and behaviour
are subjective and may be heavily influenced by the very practices covered by Article
6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925. Moreover, such perceptions and expectations may
also vary by Member State and user group and are, therefore, inadequate to assess a
service’s purpose. The purpose of a service must be assessed by reference to its
objective functionalities and tasks. Indeed, given that user perceptions are not
homogeneous, relying on the latter for determining a service’s purpose would risk
undermining the consistent interpretation of Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU)
2022/1925. It would also imply an effects-based analysis similar to what is required
for the assessment of conduct under Union competition law rules. However, as
follows, inter alia, from recitals 5 and 11 of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925, that
Regulation aims to assess the conduct of gatekeepers without requiring an effects
analysis. Put simply, the fact that certain users may be accustomed to seeing a distinct
service embedded in an OSE, and may not even perceive it as a distinct service
anymore, does not mean that such a service ceases to be objectively distinct, if it is
used for a purpose that is different to or goes beyond the purpose of an OSE.

3.2.1. The Commission’s position
(65) To determine whether there is non-compliance with Article 6(5) Regulation (EU)
1925/2022, it must be established whether there are similar third-party services on
Google Search to Alphabet’s distinct or additional services.

(66) A third-party service is similar to a distinct or additional service offered by Alphabet
when it has a similar purpose, in terms of the functionalities and tasks that it performs.
Therefore, establishing similarity necessitates a comparison of the functionalities and
tasks performed by Alphabet’s distinct or additional services, and the functionalities
and tasks performed by the services offered by third parties.
(67) As is apparent from its wording, the notion of ‘similar’ services of a third party, set out
in Article 6(5) Regulation (EU) 1925/2022, is not limited to services that are the same
or identical to services offered by the gatekeeper, but is broader.
(68) In this context, the Commission notes that the notion of ‘similar’ services does not
necessarily coincide with services belonging to the same relevant market or being
substitutable for users, within the meaning of Union competition law. As recital 11 of
Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 points out, this Regulation pursues an objective that is
complementary to, but different from that of Union competition law, which is to
protect undistorted competition on any given market. Consequently, the application of
Union competition law, including competition law precedents, is without prejudice to
the application of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925, for the purposes of establishing the
existence of similar services to those of a gatekeeper.
3.2.2. Alphabet’s arguments
(69) First, according to Alphabet, the Commission fails to establish an objective
benchmark or criteria to determine whether there are third-party services that are
similar to the separate first-party service at issue.39
(70) Second, Alphabet argues that the Commission does not clarify the conceptual
distinction between “similar services” and services that belong to the same relevant
market or are substitutable from the perspective of users.40 According to Alphabet, a
third-party service should only be considered “similar” if it serves the same purpose
for users as the gatekeeper’s service, i.e. if it is an alternative for users.41
3.2.3. The Commission’s assessment of Alphabet’s arguments
(71) First, as explained in recital (66) of this Decision, third-party services are considered
similar to the distinct or additional services offered by Alphabet on Google Search
when they serve a similar purpose. Contrary to Alphabet’s claims, the Commission
does not disregard this assessment but explains that whenever a service provides for
similar functionalities as Alphabet’s distinct or additional services, such a service
should be considered as similar. This is clearly explained and even exemplified for
each of the services assessed in this Decision.
(72) Second, the Commission disagrees with Alphabet’s position that similarity should be
equated with substitutability or the existence of alternatives in the sense it is used in
competition law. The Commission recalls that the concept of “similar services” under

(73) This interpretation is supported by recitals 5, 11, and 23 of Regulation (EU)

3.3. More favourable treatment in ranking and related indexing and crawling
3.3.1. The Commission’s position
(75) To determine whether Alphabet is treating its own distinct or additional services more
favourably in ranking and related indexing and crawling than similar services offered
by third parties, recital 52 of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 clarifies that more
favourable treatment includes “any form of differentiated or preferential treatment in
ranking (…) whether through legal, commercial or technical means” and that ranking
in this context is to be understood as “all forms of relative prominence, including
display, rating, linking or voice results”. Furthermore, recital 52 states that any
measure that has an equivalent effect to the differentiated or preferential treatment in
ranking is equally non-compliant with Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925.
(76) More favourable treatment in ranking is thus to be understood as not only including
the position in the lists of search results provided by an OSE, but also any other form
of relative prominence, given to the gatekeeper’s distinct or additional service. One
way in which a gatekeeper may favour its own distinct or additional service in ranking
occurs when the search results of an OSE contain prominent links to distinct or
additional services offered by the gatekeeper and when links to similar services
offered by third parties do not receive the same relative prominence.
(77) Other examples of such relative prominence are the frequency of display, the amount
of information displayed, the type of display features (for instance, pictures or featured
units), and the engagement possibilities for users with the content, granted to a distinct
or additional service offered by a gatekeeper, when compared to what is granted to
similar third-party services ranked on the OSE.
(78) In this context, conditioning the provision of more prominence to third parties on
requirements which do not apply to the gatekeeper’s own distinct or additional
services, does not eliminate favourable treatment. Specifically, if third-party providers

(79) According to Alphabet, the fact that Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925

(80) First, Alphabet argues that the non-discrimination obligation of Article 6(5) of
Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 is about opportunity, not outcome. Since online search

3.3.3. The Commission’s assessment of Alphabet’s arguments
(84) The Commission considers that Alphabet’s interpretation of the legal test to determine
whether there is favouring under Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 is flawed.
(85) First, the Commission agrees with Alphabet that ranking results inherently involves
treating various results differently because not all results can rank in the first place.
The Commission also agrees with Alphabet’s claim that to comply with Article 6(5) of
Regulation (EU) 2022/1925, similar services should have the same opportunity to be
shown prominently on the Google SERP. Therefore, if similar services offered by third
parties do not have the means or possibility to obtain the same prominence under the
same conditions as Alphabet’s services, the conditions for equal (not less favourable)
treatment pursuant to Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 are not met.
(86) Second, Alphabet’s claim that for proving favourable treatment, it needs to be shown
that any differential treatment produces a tangible advantage for its services and a
commensurate disadvantage for similar third-party services has no basis in the law.
(87) As set out in recital (80) of this Decision, Alphabet has correctly identified that Article
6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 is about equality of opportunity, not of outcome,
which confirms that an analysis of the effects of the prominence afforded to first- and
third-party services is not a requirement for the application of Article 6(5) of that

4. ASSESSMENT OF ALPHABET’S COMPLIANCE WITH ARTICLE 6(5) OF REGULATION (EU)
2022/1925 RELATING TO GOOGLE SEARCH FOR TRANSACTIONAL QUERIES
(90) The Commission considers that the ranking of certain of Alphabet’s services compared
to similar services offered by third parties on Google Search does not comply with
Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925.
(91) As noted in recital (26) of this Decision, Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925,
applies where (i) Alphabet offers a service that is distinct from or additional to Google
Search and that is ranked on Google Search; (ii) third parties offer similar services that
are also ranked on Google Search; and (iii) Alphabet’s services are treated more
favourably in ranking or related indexing and crawling on Google Search than those
services offered by third parties.
(92) This Decision identifies Alphabet’s non-compliance with Article 6(5) DMA regarding
Google Search in relation to nine distinct or additional services provided by Alphabet,
and which concern certain specific query types, as assessed in detail below. These
include intermediation services provided in relation to transactional queries, where
Alphabet enables the comparison of alternative offers and facilitates the initiation of
direct transactions between users and businesses, in particular, when searching for
products, flights, trains, hotels, restaurants or other physical locations.

4.1.1.1. Paid results
(95) The SERP may display a product ads unit which is filled with multiple swipeable

(96) The product ads unit is ranked based on different algorithms and criteria than those of
the free results. Free results are ranked by search algorithms based on their relevance
and quality. Paid results are ranked by search ad algorithms on the basis of relevance,
quality and an auction which takes the bid-level into account.53 Whether the product
ads unit is displayed, is determined in three steps. First, enough product ads need to
pass Alphabet’s relevance and quality thresholds to assemble a product ads unit.
Second, the eligible product ads compete for slots in the product ads unit on the basis
of an auction. Third, the product ads unit must perform better than text ads that

tests, it appears in a dedicated space on top of the SERP. If the product ads unit fails, it
does not show at all.54

4.1.2. Alphabet embeds and ranks on the SERP comparison-shopping services which are
distinct or additional to Google Search
4.1.2.1. The Commission’s position
(113) Alphabet provides two CSSs which are ranked on and embedded in the SERP but are
distinct or additional to the OSE Google Search.
4.1.2.1.1. The product ads unit
(114) As described in recitals (95) - (100) of this Decision, in response to product-related
queries, the Google SERP returns a product ads unit grouping paid search results in
the relevant product category (e.g., stand mixers as shown in Image 1). The product
ads unit, which is ranked on and embedded in Google Search, provides a distinct or an
additional service to an OSE because its purpose is different from, or in any event
goes beyond, that of an OSE. In particular, the product ads unit has specific
functionalities and performs tasks which are consistent with the purpose of a CSS,
which is to allow users to search for products and compare their prices and
characteristics across the offers of several merchants (see recital (93) of this Decision).
This is because the product ads unit presents a group of results specialised in a certain
topic with functionalities that allow users to filter, interact with, and compare
competing offers, based on relevant commercial parameters, directly on the SERP,
with a view to facilitating the initiation of transactions between businesses and
consumers.
(115) More precisely, the product ads unit groups multiple commercial offers in the product
category searched by the user and enables the search for and comparison of product
offers, as displayed in Image 2. These offers are enhanced with transactional
information such as price, provider, star rating, shipping cost and product
characteristics (e.g., energy efficiency, colour). This information is presented in a
standardised manner, facilitating the comparison of different offers intermediated by
Alphabet. Notably, the display of price information, together with other attributes and
commercial information (like shipping cost) for clearly identified products, constitute

(116) Moreover, as described in recital (104) of this Decision and shown in Image 1, the

(117) Thus, the product ads unit performs tasks consistent with the purpose of a CSS. As
explained in recital (93) of this Decision, CSSs (i) allow internet users to search for
products and compare their prices and characteristics across the offers of several
different online sellers and merchant platforms, and (ii) provide links that lead
(directly or via one or more successive intermediary pages) to the websites of such
online sellers or merchant platforms. The product ads unit connects users with CSSs
and, ultimately, with CSSs’ merchant partners. By providing information such as
prices, shipping cost, discounts and ratings, the product ads unit allows users to
compare product offers by a large range of different merchants. Furthermore, it
provides links that ultimately lead users to these merchants’ websites. The fact that
users may be directed to a third-party CSS’s website, as an intermediary step, does not
affect the nature of the product ads unit being a CSS, as further addressed in Section
4.1.2.3.3. Also, CSS ads (directing users to a CSS’s website) form an insignificant
fraction of the ads displayed in the product ads unit whereas the vast majority of slots
is taken up by standard product ads (leading directly to a merchant’s website).82
(118) In addition, the products ads unit falls outside the definition of an OSE as it does not
perform searches of, in principle, all websites or all websites in a particular language,
as explained in recitals (97) - (98) of this Decision, not all types of websites can
appear in the product ads unit; Alphabet sources this information from a specified
group of advertising partners, namely eligible CSSs and, indirectly, their merchant
partners. The information in the product ads unit is therefore not assembled by
performing searches of, in principle, all websites, but is limited to those websites that
are eligible based on the criteria pre-defined by Alphabet and provide data feeds to
Alphabet.
(119) In summary, the product ads unit presents a group of results, specialised in a specific
product category, which allows users to compare offers, including through the use of
refinement mechanisms in the form of query shortcut chips, directly on the SERP. Its
purpose therefore goes beyond the purpose of an OSE which is, in essence, to search
the Internet and deliver to users results in which information related to the requested
content can be found. Moreover, this group of results, specialised in a certain topic is

4.1.2.1.2. The products unit
(120) As described in recitals (107) - (109) of this Decision, in response to a query about
products, the Google SERP also shows a products unit, grouping product offers
relevant for that query (e.g. stand mixers). For similar reasons as for the product ads
unit, the products unit, including the preview page and the option to “View more”,
constitutes a distinct or an additional service which is ranked on and embedded in
Google Search.
(121) In particular, the purpose of the products unit is different from, or in any event goes
beyond that of an OSE, namely, it has specific functionalities and performs tasks
which are consistent with the purpose of a CSS, which is to allow users to search for
products and compare their prices and characteristics across the offers of several
merchants.
(122) Like the product ads unit, the products unit presents a group of results specialised in a
specific topic with functionalities that allow users to filter, interact with and compare
competing offers, based on relevant commercial parameters, directly on the SERP,
with a view to facilitating the initiation of transactions between businesses and
consumers.
(123) More precisely, the products unit groups commercial product offers for a given
product-related query and enables the search for and comparison of product offers.
These offers are enhanced with detailed commercial information such as swipeable
images, price, provider, colour and rating.83 It also provides a special label for
products on ‘SALE’. This information is presented in a standardised manner,
facilitating the comparison of different product offers intermediated by Alphabet.
(124) In the case of the products unit, this is reinforced by the preview page (as seen on the
right side of image 6) which resembles a product page on a CSS’s website, and which
as explained in recital (108) of this Decision, appears when clicking on any of the
product offers. On the preview page, users are provided with a wealth of product
attributes and commercial information to inform their purchase decision. This includes
images, descriptions, reviews, and videos. Further details on the products are also
included in the offer result blocks displayed in the preview page. By informing users
about the commercial information regarding different offers such as price, shipping
cost and return policy of different sales channels, the preview page facilitates the
initiating of direct transactions.
(125) Users can also refine their search by employing query shortcut chips. In addition, the
preview page may include extendable pickers allowing users to indicate e.g., their
preferred ‘colour’ in a dropdown menu. Pickers are adjusted to the product category.
When searching sneakers, for example, users can pick not only the colour but also

(128) In summary, the products unit as well as its expansion in the ‘Products’ tab constitutes
a group of results specialised in a certain topic, which allows users to compare offers,
including through the use of filtering options in the form of query shortcut chips and
the possibility to further compare different product offers in the preview page, directly
on the SERP. Its purpose is therefore to direct users to merchants’ websites and,

specialised in a certain topic, are assembled from a limited pool of websites
pre-defined and selected by Alphabet and not by performing searches of, in principle,
all websites as required by the definition of an OSE. Accordingly, Alphabet provides a
distinct or an additional service which is ranked on and embedded in Google Search.

4.1.2.3. The Commission’s assessment of Alphabet’s arguments
4.1.2.3.1. Arguments about the Commission’s analysis to determine that the products unit
and product ads unit are distinct or additional services
(158) The Commission did not err in its analysis when establishing that the products unit
and the product ads unit are distinct or additional services to Google Search for the
following reasons.
(159) First, contrary to Alphabet’s assertion, the Commission does not determine the
existence of a distinct service simply based on such service having features that are
also present in third-party services. Instead, the Commission’s assessment in this
Decision is based on an examination of whether a given group of results or dedicated
unit specialised in a certain topic present on the SERP is different or goes beyond an
OSE in terms of its purpose or the definition of an OSE. More specifically, for each of
the groups of results or dedicated units specialised in a certain topic, the Commission
assesses whether it presents a series of functionalities or performs tasks that,
individually or in combination, allow users to filter, interact with, and compare

competing offers, based on relevant commercial parameters, directly on the SERP,
with a view to facilitating the initiation of transactions between businesses and
consumers.
(160) Moreover, this assessment does not exclude the possibility that different services can
share some of the same features. In fact, as explained in recital (27) of this Decision,
all results or outputs that the OSE Google Search shows on its SERP, regardless of
their format or type and irrespective of the means through which users access such
results or the type of device they use, constitute search results. Such search results
may contain and rank services which are distinct or additional to an OSE. In other
words, contrary to Alphabet’s assertions, a specific feature shown on the SERP may at
the same time be part of an OSE and of a distinct or additional service to an OSE. The
distinguishing factor for the finding of a distinct service is not assessed based on
individual features taken in isolation but is assessed taking account of the context and
the combination of features provided. Query shortcut chips are an example of such a
feature. On the one hand, as explained in recital (59) of this Decision, when query
shortcut chips, in combination with other functionalities, are used to filter, interact
with, and compare results for a given group of search results or dedicated unit
specialised in a certain topic with a view of facilitating the initiation of transactions
between businesses and consumers, this is evidence that there is a service whose
purpose is different or goes beyond that of an OSE and, which is, therefore, distinct or
additional to an OSE. These same query shortcut chips can be used to filter
non-specialised search results on the SERP, which do not contain transaction-relevant
information, whose purpose is to search the Internet and deliver to users results in
which information related to the requested content can be found. Therefore, these
same chips can be a feature of an OSE as well as of a distinct or additional service on
the SERP.
(161) Second, contrary to Alphabet’s claim, the Commission does not exclude that, in
practice, OSEs and OISs may overlap in their features and that an OSE may facilitate
transactions. First, the Commission does not claim that products unit and product ads
unit are OISs and such an assessment and conclusion is not required to prove that a
service is distinct or additional to an OSE. However, the Commission does find that
the purpose of these distinct or additional services is that of a CSS, which is ultimately
the facilitation of initiation of transactions and which in turn is also the purpose of an
OIS. Second, as explained in recital (160) of this Decision, different services can share
some of the same features. The same applies to OSEs and OISs. Third, as explained in
recitals (55) and (56) of this Decision, the Commission bases its assessment of the
existence of a distinct service also on the fact that the legislator draws a clear legal
distinction between the notion of an OSE and that of an OIS, based on their purpose.
The broad interpretation put forward by Alphabet, according to which, in essence,
facilitating transactions would also be the purpose of an OSE, would render the legal
distinction between OSEs on the one hand, and OISs and services which have the
same purpose as OISs on the other hand, meaningless.
(162) In particular, while facilitating the initiation of direct transactions between business
users and consumers is a constitutive part of the purpose of an OIS, this might be what
an OSE incidentally does in some cases but is not a constitutive part of its purpose. As
explained in recital (58) of this Decision, it is important to make a distinction between,

41
on the one hand, enabling users to choose among search results depending on their
relevance to a user query, and, on the other, enabling users to select offers from among
products or services specialised in a certain topic, by filtering, interacting with, and
comparing them based on commercially relevant criteria, with a view to initiating a
transaction. While the first action might incidentally facilitate the initiation of direct
transactions, its purpose is to search the Internet and deliver to users results in which
information related to the requested content can be found, the second one has the
purpose of initiation of direct transactions, which goes beyond the purpose of an OSE.
(163) Third, Alphabet correctly points out that the Commission’s assessment is not based on
evidence regarding user expectations, perceptions or behaviour. This is because, as
explained in recitals (61) - (64) of this Decision, such information is subjective, may
be biased, may vary by user group and is, therefore, inadequate to assess a service’s
purpose. This purpose therefore must be assessed by reference to its objective
functionalities and tasks. The contrary would risk undermining consistent
interpretation of Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925. Furthermore, the fact that
certain users may be accustomed to seeing a distinct or additional service embedded in
an OSE does not mean that such a service ceases to be distinct from or additional to an
OSE, if it is used by end users for a purpose that is different or goes beyond the
purpose of an OSE.
(164) Additionally, Article 6(5) Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 does not require that the
product ads unit acts as a substitute for a standalone service. In line with the Annex to
Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 and the Alphabet designation decision,119 to which
Alphabet refers and which it has not contested, for the purposes of Article 6(5) of that
Regulation and in relation to the Google Search OSE, the Commission considers as
‘distinct or additional’ those services (i) that either fall in a different category of CPS
or; (ii) that serve a different purpose from that of an OSE. As explained in recitals
(114) - (119) of this Decision, the Commission found that the product ads unit serves a
different purpose from that of an OSE. The finding of a distinct or additional Alphabet
service does not require a substitutability assessment as Alphabet erroneously claims.
(165) Moreover, the Commission’s reference to recital 95 of the Alphabet Designation
Decision is relevant in this context because it sets out criteria for determining distinct
or additional services for the purposes of Article 6(5) Regulation (EU) 2022/1925.
(166) In any event, assuming that Alphabet’s evidence submitted for this purpose120 is
correct, it only suggests that users expect an OSE like Google Search to show product
ads and products units. However, this finding does not rule out that these units, in
combination with other features provided on the SERP, are distinct or additional
services to Google Search or that users do not use them for a purpose that is different
or goes beyond that of an OSE. It simply reports that users might expect to be shown a
product ads and a products unit along the results of Google Search.
(167) Fourth, the Commission’s argumentation that the products unit and the product ads
unit rely on non-crawled data, such as data feeds, indicates that those units provide
distinct or additional services, is sound. In the first place, Alphabet contradicts itself

4.1.2.3.2. Arguments about the features of the products unit and product ads unit
(168) Alphabet’s assertion set out in recitals (136) - (152) of this Decision, that the features
that the Commission lists, on their own or taken together, fail to establish that the
products unit and the product ads unit are distinct or additional services from its OSE
Google Search, is wrong. The Commission establishes that the products unit and
product ads unit are distinct or additional services to an OSE because these dedicated
units specialised in a certain topic, have functionalities and perform tasks, which taken
together go beyond the purpose of an OSE and because they fall outside the definition
of an OSE.
(169) First, the Commission does not argue that linking to suppliers’ websites is inconsistent
with the purpose of an OSE. On the contrary, as set out in recital (29) of this Decision,
the purpose of an OSE is, in essence, to search the Internet and deliver to users results
in which information related to the requested content can be found. The Commission’s
position is rather that the provision of links to merchant’s websites (directly or via a
CSSs’ website) together with specific functionalities or tasks performed directly on the
SERP by the products unit and the product ads unit is inconsistent with the purpose of
an OSE since their purpose is transactional intermediation. Moreover, these links can
only be provided by a limited pool of websites, which are pre-defined and selected by
Alphabet, instead of in principle, all websites as required by the definition of an OSE.
(170) Second, with respect to Alphabet’s argument set out in recital (139) of this Decision,
the Commission acknowledges that OSEs can and do organise search results in
varying formats, however, such search results nevertheless may be distinct or
additional to an OSE if they are specialised in a certain topic and have functionalities

(171) Regarding Alphabet’s argument about merchants considering the presentation of

(172) Third, with respect to Alphabet’s argument in recital (140) of this Decision, the

Therefore, regardless of whether transaction-related information helps users to better

are unfair.
