explained in recital (58) of this Decision, there is a distinction to be made between, on

44
the one hand, enabling users to choose among search results depending on their
relevance to a user query and, on the other enabling users to select among product
offers from merchants and CSSs, based on the same commercial parameters with a
view of initiating transactions. As described in recital (93) of this Decision, CSSs
allow users to compare products across number of different online sellers on the basis
of their prices and other product-specific characteristics. The product unit and product
ads units have exactly those functionalities and perform those tasks.
(176) Fifth, contrary to what Alphabet is alleging, the Commission does not consider that
sourcing data via data feeds is not consistent with the purpose of an OSE per se.
Instead, the Commission notes that, as explained in recital (60) of this Decision, a
distinct or additional service to an OSE is shown when a given dedicated unit
specialised in a certain topic is not assembled by performing searches of, in principle,
all websites. In this case, in response to a product-related query, the product ads and
products units show results obtained from a limited pool of websites pre-defined and
selected by Alphabet and that have opted in to providing data feeds to Alphabet as
explained in recital (118) of this Decision. Therefore, the decisive factor for finding of
a distinct service in this case is the fact that the dedicated units in question are
assembled based on data feeds that are provided by a limited pool of websites
pre-defined and selected by Alphabet instead of by searching, in principle, all
websites. In addition, as explained in recital (118) Alphabet sources information from
CSSs and therefore, information in the product ads unit is not assembled by
performing searches of, in principle, all websites as required by the definition of an
OSE.
(177) Sixth, as regards Alphabet’s argument in recital (144) of this Decision that the data for
the search results shown in response to a particular query comes only from relevant
websites and not from “all websites”, the Commission notes that, as explained in
recital (53) of this Decision, returning results from in principle all websites, limited
only to the extent they have some relationship to a user’s query, is not the same as
presenting grouped results or dedicated units in a specific topic, which systematically
show information not sourced from ‘in principle, all websites’ and whose purpose is to
compare offers and thereby facilitate initiation of transactions. More precisely, the
products and product ads unit inherently and only show results retrieved from
merchants and CSSs’ websites, since, as set out in recital (126) of this Decision, only
CSSs who have opted into providing data feeds to Alphabet are eligible to participate
in the offer result blocks contained in the products unit, and only CSS websites who
have successfully applied previously to Alphabet’s CSS program can place product
ads in the product ads unit. This means that, regardless of the query, these units are
never populated by searching ‘in principle, all websites’. Furthermore, as described in
recitals (114) - (118) and (122) - (127) the fact that these units are assembled based on
data feeds from a limited pool of websites, allows for a comparison of
transaction-relevant information within those units, which goes beyond the purpose of
an OSE..
(178) Seventh, regarding Alphabet’s arguments about query shortcut chips set out in recitals
(145) - (147) of this Decision, the Commission notes that, as explained in recital (59)
of this Decision, the availability of query shortcut chips to users is indicative of the
existence of a distinct or additional service to an OSE because these chips, in

45
combination with other functionalities, allow users to perform tasks which go beyond
the purpose of an OSE.
(179) Indeed, as regards the product ads unit and the products unit, the Commission notes
that, as explained in recitals (116) and (125) of this Decision, query shortcut chips
provide an additional means to interact with these units and, in particular, to filter
transaction-relevant information, thereby adding CSS-like functionalities to the units
and performing tasks of a CSS.
(180) In the first place, the fact that query shortcut chips can serve as a means to input
search queries without having to type as set out in recital (146) of this Decision, has no
bearing on the assessment of whether such chips can also be used to filter and compare
product offers on the basis of relevant parameters.
(181) In the second place, regarding Alphabet’s argument in recital (147) of this Decision
that certain stakeholders believe query shortcut chips to be an important part of an
OSE and that OSEs have provided such a functionality since 2003, the fact remains
that, as explained in recitals (28) and (32) of this Decision, one of the decisive factors
for the assessment to determine whether a service is distinct or additional service to an
OSE is by reference to its purpose, in particular in terms of the functionalities and
tasks that the service in question performs and not subjective perceptions or beliefs.
The data from the last 15 years show that Alphabet has consistently held a very large
share of the European search market, remaining between roughly 88–95% throughout
the entire period.123 Therefore users have become deeply accustomed to how Google
Search looks and operates, and that they might expect to be shown query shortcut
chips on the SERP. However, this finding does not rule out that these chips, in
combination with other features of the units in question, turn these units into distinct
or additional services to Google Search or that users do not use them for a purpose that
is different or goes beyond that of an OSE.
(182) In the third place, contrary to Alphabet’s claims, query shortcut chips allow users to
filter and narrow down the offers displayed in the products unit and product ads unit.
Because these units only include results from a limited type and pool of websites as set
out in section 4.1.1 and in recital (118) of this Decision, interactions with query
shortcut chips do narrow down the pool of results shown. This is also evident when
one searches for e.g., a “kitchen mixer” on Google Search. Once such query is issued
and “Smeg” query shortcut chip is selected, products unit presents only Smeg (brand)
kitchen mixers. This indeed proves that those chips interact with the product ads and
products units by filtering the results.
(183) In the fourth place, regardless of how often users click on query shortcut chips, the
functionality itself is designed to allow users to select multiple chips to refine and
filter their results continuously on the SERP.
(184) Lastly, regarding Alphabet’s argument that it only includes eight query shortcut chips
it must be noted that new query shortcut chips are displayed following every
refinement of a query, which compounds the number of chips shown for each query.
The initial number of query shortcut chips displayed is therefore not determinative for
the assessment.

(185) Eighth, Alphabet’s claim set out in recitals (150) - (152) of this Decision that neither
the product unit, nor the product ads unit provide full functionality of an OIS and,
therefore, are not distinct from Google Search, is incorrect.
(186) In the first place, as explained in recital (54) of this Decision, the Commission does
not claim that the product unit or product ads unit are OISs. Nevertheless, the
Commission does not exclude that, in practice, an overlap may exist between OSEs
and other distinct services. The assessment whether a particular service may be
qualified as an OSE or as other type of distinct or additional service must be carried
out, in particular, in light of the purpose of such services. In this case, the specific
functionalities or tasks performed by the products unit and product ads unit are
inconsistent with the purpose of an OSE as set out in recitals (113) - (128) of this
Decision.
(187) In the second place, Alphabet’s argument that the products unit and product ads unit
are not distinct from Google Search because they do not have any separate means for
users to issue a query to Alphabet’s distinct CSSs nor have any separate mechanisms
to filter or sort results in the units, is irrelevant as it is not determinative for finding of
a distinct or additional service. In fact, as set out in recital 51 of Regulation (EU)
2022/1925 distinct or additional services may be partly or entirely embedded in or
displayed along search results. Therefore, the fact that an OSE and a distinct or
additional service, which is partly or entirely embedded in its search results use the
same means to issue queries, or filter and sort results cannot by itself imply that such a
service is not distinct or additional.
4.1.2.3.3. Arguments about the products unit and product ads unit being a means to show
better results
(188) The Commission disagrees with Alphabet’s view that the product ads unit serves the
purpose of an OSE. While the Commission does not contest that the unit helps users
find products corresponding to their query, the purpose of the product ads unit goes
beyond searching the Internet and delivering to users results in which information
related to the requested content can be found. As explained in recital (119) of this
Decision, the unit has specific functionalities and performs tasks that enable not only
the search for product offers but also their comparison directly on the SERP. This is
not called into question by Alphabet’s arguments.
(189) First, it is not decisive for the application of Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU)
2022/1925 whether Alphabet’s own service is beneficial to one user group or another.
The legislator deliberately opted against allowing for this sort of efficiency defence in
the application of that Regulation.124 In any event, as set out in Section 10 of this
Decision, Alphabet is not required to remove the product ads unit altogether. To
comply with Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925, it would be sufficient for

(190) Second, the alleged expectation by users that Google Search shows product ads does
not prevent the application of Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925.
(191) In the first place, as explained in recitals (61) - (64) of this Decision, the delineation
between services is a legal question rather than an empirical one. The Commission
applied an objectivised test to determine the purpose of the product ads unit from a
user perspective. To this end, the Commission examined the purpose by reference to
the functionalities and tasks performed by the service in question (see recital (28) of
this Decision).
(192) In the second place, a service can be distinct from Google Search regardless of
whether users expect to find it there. In the same vein, YouTube and Google Maps are
distinct from Google Search although they commonly feature on the SERP.
(193) In the third place, as emphasised by Alphabet itself, Google Search displays and
develops product ads since 2008 and has not ceased doing so by the time of
adoption.125 If a long-standing integration of services with Google Search would mean
that these services are no longer distinct, the application of Article 6(5) of Regulation
(EU) 2022/1925 could be entirely undermined by a gatekeeper’s past practice even if
such practice became unlawful.
(194) Third, the Commission disagrees with Alphabet’s view that the product ads unit does
not constitute a CSS.
(195) In the first place, the product ads unit allows users to compare products regardless of
whether the offers are brokered by CSSs through whose websites the clicks are routed.
Accordingly, the General Court confirmed that a CSS may “provide links that lead
(directly or via one or more successive intermediary pages)” to the websites of online
sellers or merchant platforms.126 Unlike Alphabet suggests, the General Court did not
simply refer to the Commission’s definition of a CSS. The General Court found that
“[i]n the present case, it is appropriate to adopt the definition of a comparison
shopping service […], which, moreover, has not been called into question by
Google”.127 While it is true that Alphabet tweaked the product ads unit in the
meantime, these changes do not take the product ads unit outside the scope of the
definition of a CSS.
(196) In the second place, the distinction between the OSE Google Search and the product
ads unit is not called into question by Alphabet’s reference to the Court of Justice’s
ruling. A comprehensive reading of the quote reveals that product ads “do not
constitute an infrastructure that is separate from [Google Search] in the sense of an

4.1.3. Third parties offer similar services which are ranked on the SERP
4.1.3.1. The Commission’s position
(198) When a user submits a product-related search query on third-party CSSs’ websites
they are presented with a display of the product, which typically includes
functionalities such as product image, customer ratings and reviews, prices from
different suppliers, delivery options and links to direct suppliers of the specific
product. In addition, users can apply filters when they search for products on CSSs
websites. These filters typically allow users to narrow down or refresh product
searches based on various criteria like price, brand, ratings, sizes or availability (or
other criteria depending on the specific product query). Examples of such CSSs
include Ceneo, Guenstiger, Idealo, Kelkoo and Trovaprezzi.
(199) As noted in recitals (117) to (127) of this Decision, functionalities offered by
third-party CSSs following product-related query are similar to the functionalities of
the Alphabet’s CSSs embedded and ranked on the Google SERP. As also noted in
recital (120) of this Decision, a third-party service is similar to a distinct or additional
service offered by Alphabet when it has a similar purpose.
(200) The definition of an OSE in Article 2, point (5), of Regulation (EU) 2019/1150, which
is referred to in Article 2, point (6), of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 includes results of,
“in principle, all websites”. Given that third-party CSSs rely on OSEs to reach users,
their websites are ranked on the SERP, absent any opt-out, following a product-related
query to which they provide relevant results. This is because OSEs provide results
based on searches performed, in principle, on all websites.
4.1.3.2. Alphabet’s arguments
(201) According to Alphabet, the Commission overlooks relevant differences between the
result units at issue and the allegedly similar third-party services, which according to
Alphabet, invalidates the Commission’s favouring allegations.129
(202) First, Alphabet claims that the Commission does not maintain that Google's result
units at issue provide all functionalities of the purported similar third-party services.
According to Alphabet, the difference in functionality is a relevant factor for

49
determining whether a first-party service obtains an advantage from the display of the
units and whether this is compensated by the March 2024 changes.130
(203) Second, Alphabet argues that the Commission does not establish that the result units at
issue are a substitute to third-party services. There is no good reason, according to
Alphabet, why results that address different user demand should be treated
identically.131
(204) Third, Alphabet states that Google's result units for suppliers treat suppliers
fundamentally differently from third-party CSSs. The results in Google's supplier units
are free for suppliers and open to them. Whereas to appear in these results, suppliers
must pay CSSs, and users only get to see results from those paying suppliers. It is
wrong, according to Alphabet, to demand that third-party CSSs, should be treated
equally with the supplier units at issue, since the CSSs results operate differently.132
4.1.3.3. The Commission’s assessment of Alphabet’s arguments
(205) First, the Commission rejects Alphabet’s assertion that it ignored relevant differences
between the result units at issue and similar third-party services. As explained in
recital (66) of this Decision, third-party services are considered similar when they
allow users to serve equivalent purposes as those of Alphabet’s additional services
displayed on Google Search. The notion of a “similar service” does not rule out that
certain differences between the services exist.133
(206) Second, the Commission recalls that as set out in recital (68) of this Decision, the
concept of “similar services” under Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 does
not coincide with the notion of substitutability used in Union competition law. It is not
required that services belong to the same relevant market or are considered as
substitute by users. The legislative choice of the term “similar” allows the
Commission to focus its assessment based on the purpose of the service bearing in
mind the concept of “similar services”.
(207) Third, the Commission disagrees with Alphabet’s claim that the difference in
monetisation between its own result units and similar services offered by third parties
is material for the assessment under Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925.
Actually, the difference on monetisation models is a result of the vertical integration of
Alphabet because it offers an OSE for which it has been designated as a gatekeeper
and can monetise its embedded CSSs by selling advertising, whereas providers of
similar services cannot monetise their services in this way. The analysis under Article
6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 does not turn on chosen business model of the
third-party but rather on whether the third-party service as a whole performs a
comparable task for users. As long as both services allow users to perform comparable
tasks—such as facilitating the comparison and selection of product offers —they can
be considered similar, regardless of their business model.

4.1.4. More favourable treatment in ranking on the SERP of Alphabet’s product ads unit
and products unit
4.1.4.1. The Commission’s position
(208) When entering a product-related query, Alphabet’s product ads unit and its products
unit are given more favourable treatment in ranking on Google Search, as compared to
third-party CSSs.
(209) Both Alphabet’s product ads unit and its products unit are embedded and ranked
prominently on Google Search.
(210) First, Alphabet’s product ads unit is embedded in the SERP and can be seen by a user
immediately after entering a product-related query. It is displayed at the top of the
SERP, which makes it especially visible for users navigating through the SERP. The
product ads unit, which contains paid search results delivered in response to a
product-related query, consists of a large, dedicated box displaying detailed
information in relation to e.g., prices, shipping costs, ratings, energy efficiency, and
other characteristics of products offered on CSS websites. This enables users, in the
product ads unit itself (i.e., directly on the SERP, immediately after entering a
product-related query), to search and compare several different products offered on
CSS websites with a view to initiating a transaction.
(211) Second, Alphabet’s products unit is also embedded in the SERP and can be seen by a
user immediately after entering a product-related query. The products unit, which
contains free search results delivered in response to a product-related query, consists
of a dedicated box displaying information in relation to e.g., prices and star ratings of
several products offered by merchants. This enables users, in the products unit itself
(i.e., directly on the SERP, immediately after entering a product-related query), to
search and compare several different products offered by merchants with a view to
initiating a transaction.
(212) Additionally, when a user clicks on one of the results in the products unit, it is then
presented with a preview page containing further information about the product at
issue including, in addition to more images, information on e.g., availability, prices,
ratings, shipping costs, and return policies. This preview page, which contains offers
from both merchants and CSSs, enables users to carry out a further comparison of
different products offered by merchants and CSSs. Also, the search results which are
displayed following a click on the ‘Products’ tab or on the ‘View more’ or ‘View more
products’ button (placed at the bottom of the products unit) contain more merchant
offers displaying the same type of transaction-relevant information as the products
unit. Additionally, the search results which are displayed following a click on the
‘Products’ tab also contain the product ads unit with the same characteristics.
(213) Third-party CSSs also have opportunities to feature on the SERP. However, they
feature less prominently, as compared to Alphabet’s embedded products unit and
product ads unit.
(214) As regards free search results, first, it is true that a third-party CSS may display offers
in the products unit’s preview page (albeit not in the products unit itself), and that this
preview page is accessible once a user clicks on one of the results in the products unit.
However, for a third-party CSS, eligibility to potentially display individual offers in

51
the preview page is not the same as having its own box, embedded in the SERP and
visible immediately after entering a product-related query, containing several product
offerings from its inventory that a user can compare directly on the SERP, as is the
case for Alphabet with its products unit. Conditioning equal prominence on
requirements that do not apply to the gatekeeper’s own services is not granting equal
prominence on the SERP. In order to gain some prominence on the SERP, third-party
CSSs have to become business partners of Alphabet’s products unit instead of being
able to display their own inventory on equal terms on the SERP. Therefore, Alphabet’s
CSS is favoured compared to third-party CSSs on the SERP.
(215) Second, a third-party CSS may also appear in free organic search results, be it rich
web results or ordinary (i.e., non-rich) results.
(216) It is true that rich web results, which have an enhanced format, containing both images
as well as information on the products at issue, also enable a third-party CSS to
present several product offerings in an embedded box. However, overall, the
possibility for a CSS to feature in rich web results does not compensate for the
prominence given to Alphabet’s products unit. This is because the prominence of the
products unit is strengthened by additional features which provide users with more
possibilities to compare products with a view to initiating a transaction. In particular,
as stated above, contrary to rich web results, the products unit gives users access to a
preview page (accessible by clicking on one of the results in the products unit), which
contains not only more images, but also more detailed information on e.g., availability,
prices, ratings, shipping costs, and return policies. Additionally, the products unit has,
at the bottom, a ‘View more’ or ‘View more products’ button that directs users
towards more merchant offers displaying the same type of transaction-relevant
information, as does the ‘Products’ tab located at the top of the SERP.
(217) Ordinary (i.e., non-rich) results, in turn, do not offer a third-party CSS a degree of
prominence comparable to that of Alphabet’s embedded products unit, as they do not
contain images or structured product-related information, and do not enable a CSS to
present different product offerings that a user can compare directly on the SERP.
(218) Third, the possibility for a third-party CSS to feature in the CSS unit and in the
‘Product comparison sites’ tab does not give it equal prominence as compared to
Alphabet’s products unit either.
(219) The CSS unit does not allow a given CSS to have its own box, embedded in the SERP
and visible immediately after entering a product-related query, containing several
product offerings that a user can compare directly on the SERP.
(220) The possibility for a third-party CSS to include a link within the ‘Product comparison
sites’ tab is not the same as it having its own box, embedded in the SERP and visible
immediately after entering a product-related query, containing several product
offerings that a user can compare directly on the SERP. Additionally, it is noteworthy
that, while there are no tabs for individual third-party CSSs displayed on top of the
SERP, which would link to and show only the offers from their respective inventory,
the results in the ‘Products tab’ are an extended version of those displayed in
Alphabet’s products unit. Given that the ‘Product comparison sites’ tab shows the
results of various CSSs, it gives less prominence to individual third-party CSSs

52
compared to the ‘Products’ tab, which exclusively shows results of Alphabet’s
products unit.
(221) As regards paid search results, first, while it is true that a third-party CSS may display
ads directly on the SERP in the product ads unit, this does not give them equal
prominence as compared to Alphabet’s product ads unit. Indeed, this is not the same as
having their own box, embedded in the SERP and visible immediately after entering a
product-related query, containing several product offerings that a user can compare
directly on the SERP.
(222) Second, a third-party CSS may also obtain visibility by placing CLAs. However, these
ads promote a CSS website as a whole, but do not provide a third-party CSS with an
embedded box or unit on the SERP, containing several product offerings that a user
can compare directly on the SERP. The CLA unit is only displayed when a user clicks
on the tab ‘Comparison Sites’ on top of the product ads unit, and is thus not visible
directly on the SERP, immediately after entering a product-related query.
(223) For the reasons stated above, the Commission concludes that Alphabet gives its
products unit and its product ads unit more favourable treatment in ranking on Google
Search, as compared to similar services offered by third parties.

(224) Alphabet argues that even if the products and product ads units at issue were qualified
as distinct services that are similar to third-party CSSs, the Commission’s position that
Alphabet improperly favours its first-party services on the SERP is invalid.134

CSS’ inventory in the result. Alphabet claims that rich web results for CSSs in fact
give each CSS their ‘own box’ where they can showcase multiple offers from their
inventory.137

(261) First, as regards Alphabet’s arguments set out in recitals (240) - (243) of this Decision

which the Commission finds that Alphabet’s products unit gets more prominence on
the SERP than similar third-party services. Alphabet’s arguments fail to challenge this.
(262) In the first place, Alphabet’s argument in recital (242) of this Decision that enabling
users to compare is intrinsic to OSEs and not specific to CSSs challenges the
Commission’s finding that Alphabet embeds its distinct CSS on the SERP rather than
the prominence in ranking provided to the products unit relative to third-party CSSs
and has been addressed in recital (175) of this Decision.
(263) In the second place, Alphabet’s argument set out in recital (243) of this Decision
correctly identifies that the Commission does not explain how allowing comparison of
product offers directly on the SERP benefits an Alphabet CSS. This is the case
because as set out in recital (86) of this Decision, contrary to what Alphabet argues,
the assessment of compliance with Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 does
not require the Commission to establish a tangible advantage for Alphabet’s distinct or
additional services.
(264) Nevertheless, some of Alphabet’s claims to support this argument are addressed in
order to correct them. Namely, Alphabet’s contention that no traffic for Alphabet’s
CSS is generated because there are no links to an Alphabet CSS in the products unit
ignores that the products unit itself obtains traffic by being prominently shown on the
SERP and allowing users to use Alphabet’s CSS without having to leave the SERP.
Additionally, the fact that merchants can choose whether or not to also have their data
used in Alphabet’s CSSs on other domains than Google Search, means that some may
choose to do so, thereby giving further benefits to Alphabet’s own distinct or
additional services by increasing the data available to its CSS. Alphabet’s argument
that it is more advantageous for third-party CSSs when users are led to their website
than to allowing them to provide comparison directly on Google Search was already
addressed in recital (258) of this Decision.
(265) Second, as regards Alphabet’s arguments in relation to the product ads unit, the
relevant legal test assesses the relative prominence of first- and third-party services,
not about the revenue made or other outcome variables. Alphabet’s arguments about
equal treatment and the product ads unit set out in recital (244) of this Decision were
already addressed in recitals (259) and (260) of this Decision.
4.1.4.3.3. Arguments about taking into account stakeholder interests
(266) Alphabet’s claim set out in recitals (245) of this Decision that the Commission fails to
consider the interests of merchants and instead focuses on the interests of CSSs is
false. As emphasised by Alphabet, the Commission participated in multiple workshops

60
and meetings with both merchants and CSSs and recognises the need to balance
stakeholder interests when applying Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925.
Therefore, contrary to what Alphabet claims, the Commission does not disregard
merchants’ interests and, as explained in recital (89) of this Decision, is cognisant of
the need to take into account Alphabet’s other obligations under Regulation (EU)
2022/1925 and to respect the general principle of proportionality when assessing
Alphabet’s measures to comply with the obligation in Article 6(5) of that Regulation.
At the same time, assessing whether there is equal treatment in ranking, the
comparison in prominence applies to Alphabet’s distinct or additional services and
similar services of third parties, not of any business user of the OSE in general.
4.1.5. Conclusion
(267) The Commission therefore takes the view that Alphabet offers two product
intermediation services that are distinct from or additional to Google Search and that
those services are more favourably ranked on the SERP than similar services of third
parties.

4.2.2.4. Arguments about the features of the airlines unit

not demonstrate that the airlines unit constitute distinct or additional service. For the

4.2.2.4.1. Arguments about the airlines unit being a means to show better results
(290) The Commission disagrees with Alphabet’s view that the airlines unit serves the
purpose of an OSE. As explained in recital (280) of this Decision, the unit offers
features and performs tasks that enable not only the search for airlines but also
comparison.
(291) First, as noted in recital (189) of this Decision, it is not decisive for the application of
Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 whether Alphabet’s own service is
beneficial to one user group or another. In any event, in order to comply with this
Decision Alphabet is not required to remove the airlines unit altogether.
(292) Second, the Commission does not agree with Alphabet’s distinction between flight
offers and airline results. As explained in recital (272) of this Decision and not
contested by Alphabet, the “indicative price” reflects the minimum price offered by an
airline on a given date. The interplay between minimum prices and further information
enables users to compare airlines in search for the most suitable offer. To this end,
users do not require information on upgrades such as a higher seat class or checked
baggage. As a matter of fact, third-party VSSs like Skyscanner do not offer these
upgrades either. Instead, they direct users to the airline’s website to customise their
flight, just like the airlines unit does.
4.2.3. Third parties offer similar services which are ranked on the SERP
4.2.3.1. The Commission’s position
(293) Third parties offer services, which have similar functionalities to those of Alphabet’s
flight intermediation service that is ranked on and embedded in the SERP. These
third-party flight VSSs are ranked on the SERP in various ways. OSEs provide results
based on search performed of, in principle, all websites, absent any opt-out.
(294) This is the case, for example, for VSSs intermediating flights, such as Kayak, Expedia,
Skyscanner, eDreams or FareCompare. VSSs like these, typically share common
functionalities, such as the display of transaction-relevant information, including the
flight operator, pricing, whether the flight is connecting or not. They allow users to
search for specific flight dates, filter results based on preferences such as price, round
trip, duration, or number of stops and allow users to search for flights across various
operators.
(295) As noted in recital (275) of this Decision, Alphabet’s flight intermediation service is
similar to these VSSs offered by third parties as it also displays transaction-relevant

67
information, namely, flight operator, prices and whether the flight is connecting or not.
Just like third-party VSSs, Alphabet’s flight intermediation service provides the users
with means to refine their flight-related search query by, for example, filtering for the
cheapest flight, a specific date, round trip or operator. As also noted in recital (274) of
this Decision, a third-party service is similar to a distinct or additional service offered
by Alphabet when it has a similar purpose, i.e., to facilitate the initiation of direct
transactions.
(296) For these reasons, the Commission concludes that third parties offer services, which
are ranked on Google Search, and which are similar to the additional service, namely,
the flight intermediation service, provided by Alphabet on the SERP.
4.2.3.2. Alphabet’s arguments
(297) According to Alphabet, the Commission overlooks relevant differences between the
result units at issue and the allegedly similar third-party services, which according to
Alphabet, invalidates the Commission’s favouring allegations.175 To support this claim,
Alphabet brings forward the same arguments as for the products and product ads unit
as set out in recitals (201) – (204) of this Decision.
4.2.3.3. The Commission’s assessment of Alphabet’s arguments
(298) First, the Commission rejects Alphabet’s assertion that it ignored relevant differences
between the result units at issue and similar third-party services, as also explained in
recital (205) of this Decision. It is sufficient that the result units have certain
functionalities that facilitate the initiation of transaction.
(299) Second, the Commission recalls that as set out in recital (206) of this Decision, the
concept of “similar services” under Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 does
not coincide with the notion of substitutability used in Union competition law.
(300) Third, the Commission disagrees with Alphabet’s claim that the difference in
monetisation between its own result units and similar services offered by third parties
is material for the assessment under Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 as
explained in recital (207) of this Decision.
4.2.4. More favourable treatment in ranking on the SERP of Alphabet’s flights
intermediation service
4.2.4.1. The Commission’s position
(301) When entering a flights-related query, Alphabet’s own flights intermediation service is
given more favourable treatment in ranking on Google Search, as compared to similar
services offered by third parties.
(302) First, Alphabet’s flights intermediation service is embedded and ranked prominently
on the SERP in the form of the airlines unit in combination with query shortcut chips.
It consists of a dedicated box displaying transaction-relevant information such as
prices of several flights offered by airlines. This enables users, in the flight’s unit
itself, to search and compare several different flights offered by airlines with a view to
initiating a transaction.

(303) Second, users have the possibility to access the extended version of Alphabet’s flights
intermediation service directly from the SERP by clicking on the ‘Airline options’ tab
displayed on top of the SERP or via the ‘More airline options’ button at the bottom of
the airlines unit.
(304) VSSs intermediating flights also have opportunities to feature on the SERP. They can
appear in rich web results, dedicated VSS unit as well as following a click on the VSS
tab and ‘More flight sites’ button at the bottom of the VSS unit. However, third-party
VSSs intermediating flights feature less prominently on the SERP than Alphabet’s
flights intermediation service for the following reasons.
(305) First, the possibility of VSSs to feature in rich web results does not compensate for the
prominence given to Alphabet’s flights intermediation service in the form of the
airlines unit. Third-party VSSs are not given the possibility to display their own
airlines unit, which would interact with the filters contained in query shortcut chips,
anywhere on the SERP. While rich web results allow for a display of one single flight
offer by a third-party VSSs directly on the SERP, unlike the airlines unit, they do not
allow for comparison of several flights offered by the same VSS based on
transaction-relevant information. Moreover, rich web results for VSSs are not
displayed as prominently in terms of size as the airlines unit.
(306) Second, the possibility of VSSs to feature in the VSS unit does not compensate for the
prominence given to Alphabet’s flights intermediation service in the form of the
airlines unit. The VSS unit does not allow a given VSS to have its own box, embedded
on the SERP and visible immediately after entering a flights-related query, containing
several airline offers.
(307) Third, there is no reserved link to any other VSS that intermediates flights on the
SERP as is the case for the link to an extended version of the airlines unit, which is
included at the bottom of the latter. The ’More flight sites’ link, which is at the bottom
of the VSS unit, presents to the user results of various VSSs and, therefore, does not
give individual VSSs the same prominence as the prominence given to Alphabet’s
service via the link reserved for it at the bottom of the airlines unit. Similarly, the VSS
tab does not compensate for the prominence given to Alphabet’s flight intermediation
service through the ‘Flights’ tab. There are no tabs for individual third-party VSSs
displayed on top of the SERP, which would link to and show only the offers and
functionalities from their respective inventory as is the case for Alphabet’s flight
intermediation service via the ‘Flights’ tab. Given that the VSS tab shows the results
of various VSSs it gives less prominence to individual third party VSSs compared to
the ‘Flights’ tab, which exclusively shows results of Alphabet’s own flights
intermediation service.
(308) For the reasons stated above, the Commission concludes that Alphabet gives its flights
intermediation service more favourable treatment in ranking on Google Search,
compared to similar services offered by third parties.

4.3.2. Alphabet’s trains intermediation service is distinct or additional to Google Search
and is ranked on the SERP
4.3.2.1. The Commission’s position
(325) As described in recital (323) of this Decision, in response to train-related queries, the
Google SERP shows a trains unit. This unit, which is ranked on and embedded in
Google Search, provides a distinct or an additional service to an OSE because its
purpose goes beyond that of an OSE, namely, it has functionalities and performs tasks,
which are consistent with the purpose of a VSS
(326) In particular, the trains unit presents a group of results specialised in a certain topic
with functionalities that allow users to filter, interact with, and compare competing
offers based on relevant commercial parameters, directly on the SERP, with a view to
facilitating the initiation of transactions between businesses and consumers.
(327) More precisely, by featuring transactional information, the trains unit enables the
search for and comparison of train itinerary offers based on different commercial
factors such as prices, trip duration, times of departure and arrival and number of
changes. Clicking on one of the train options in the unit expands to show further
details for that trip.
(328) Furthermore, as described in recital (322) of this Decision and shown in Images 10
and 11, the SERP provides query shortcut chips that allow users to filter the
information in the trains unit and select, for example, whether they are searching for a
‘Direct’ train itinerary while the ‘Dates’, ‘Times’ and ‘Train station’ pickers allow
them to choose exact date, times and train stations of their choice. As Alphabet states
itself, query shortcut chips operate as ‘filters’.186
(329) In addition, the trains unit falls outside the definition of an OSE as it does not perform
searches of in principle all websites, or all websites in a particular language. As
described in recital (323) of this Decision, not all types of websites can appear in the
trains unit; only train ticket vendors’ websites can. Additionally, to be eligible to
feature in this unit, train ticket vendors have to provide data feeds to Alphabet. As
explained by Alphabet, data feeds enable a more accurate display of
transaction-relevant data, in particular, of real-time prices for train itineraries.187 The
trains unit and the comparison enabled within is, therefore, not assembled by
performing searches of, in principle, all websites, but is limited to those websites that
are train ticket vendors’ websites and that provide data feeds to Alphabet based on a
pre-defined set of Alphabet’s criteria.
(330) The search results, which are displayed following a click on the ‘Trains’ tab on top of
the SERP or the ‘More results’ button at the bottom of the trains unit, contain more of

the train travel offers displaying the same type of transaction-relevant information as

(331) In summary, the trains unit displayed on the SERP, as well as the results page which is
displayed following a click on the ‘Trains’ tab or the ‘More results’ button, presents a
group of results specialised in a certain topic which allows users to compare offers,
including through refinement chips, for a specific train-travel related query, directly on
the SERP. Their purpose is, therefore, to facilitate the initiation of direct transactions,
which goes beyond the purpose of an OSE, which is, in essence, to search the Internet
and deliver to users results in which information related to the requested content can
be found. Moreover, these groups of results, specialised in a certain topic are
assembled from a limited pool of websites pre-defined and selected by Alphabet and
not by performing searches of, in principle, all websites as required by the definition
of an OSE. For these reasons, Alphabet provides a distinct or an additional train
intermediation service directly ranked on and embedded in the SERP.
(332) For the reasons stated above, the Commission concludes that Alphabet offers a distinct
or an additional train intermediation service, via Google Search.

4.3.3. Third parties offer similar services which are ranked on the SERP
4.3.3.1. The Commission’s position
(344) Third parties offer services, which have similar functionalities to those of Alphabet’s
train intermediation service that is ranked on and embedded in the SERP. These
third-party train travel VSSs, such as Rail Europe, Trainline, Omio, TrainPal or
HappyRail are ranked on the SERP in various ways. This is because OSEs provide
results based on search performed of, in principles, all websites, absent any opt-out.
They can appear as organic search result on the SERP or in the VSS unit as explained
in recital (324) of this Decision.
(345) VSSs like the ones mentioned, offer platforms for users to find and compare train
travel options. They typically share common features such as display of
transaction-relevant information: pricing, train schedules and number of stops. They
allow users to search for specific train travel dates, filter results based on preferences
such as price, train ticket vendor or number of stops and allow users to search for train
itineraries across various train operators and vendors.
(346) Alphabet’s train intermediation service is similar to these VSSs offered by third parties
as it also displays transaction-relevant information, namely, prices, number of changes
and trip duration. Just like third-party VSSs, it provides users with the means to refine
their train-travel search query by, for example, filtering for a specific date, time or
direct itineraries only.
(347) For these reasons, the Commission concludes that third parties offer services, which
are ranked on Google Search and which are similar to the additional service, namely,
train intermediation service, provided by Alphabet on the SERP.
4.3.3.2. Alphabet’s arguments
(348) According to Alphabet, the Commission overlooks relevant differences between the
result units at issue and the allegedly similar third-party services, which according to
Alphabet, invalidates the Commission’s favouring allegations.192 To support this claim,
Alphabet brings forward the same arguments as for the products and product ads unit
as set out in recitals (201) - (204) of this Decision.
4.3.3.3. The Commission’s assessment of Alphabet’s arguments
(349) First, the Commission rejects Alphabet’s assertion that it ignored relevant differences
between the result units at issue and similar third-party services, as also explained in

4.3.4. More favourable treatment in ranking on the SERP of Alphabet’s trains
intermediation service
4.3.4.1. The Commission’s position
(352) When entering a query related to train itinerary, Alphabet’s own train intermediation
service is given more favourable treatment in ranking on Google Search, as compared
to similar services offered by third parties.
(353) First, Alphabet’s train intermediation service is embedded and ranked prominently on
the SERP in the form of the trains unit in combination with query shortcut chips. It
consists of a large, dedicated box displaying transaction-relevant information such as
prices of several train itineraries offered by railways. This enables users, in the trains
unit itself, to search and compare several different train itineraries offered by railways
with a view to initiating a transaction.
(354) Second, users have the possibility to expand the different train itinerary options
displayed in the trains unit and thereby obtain further transaction-relevant information
related to the chosen itinerary directly on the SERP.
(355) Third, users have the possibility to access the extended version of Alphabet’s train
intermediation service directly from the SERP by clicking on the ‘Trains’ tab
displayed on top of the SERP.
(356) Fourth, the prominence of Alphabet’s train intermediation service is also strengthened
by users having the possibility to access it via the ‘More results’ button at the bottom
of the trains unit.
(357) VSSs intermediating train travel also have opportunities to feature on the SERP. They
can appear in the dedicated VSS unit and following a click on the VSS tab and ‘More
results’ button at the bottom of the VSS unit.
(358) However, third party train travel VSSs feature less prominently on the SERP than
Alphabet’s train intermediation service for the following reasons.
(359) First, the possibility of VSSs to feature in the VSS unit does not compensate for the
prominence given to Alphabet’s train intermediation service in the form of the trains
unit. The VSS unit does not allow a given VSSs to have its own box, embedded on the
SERP and visible immediately after entering a train travel related query, containing
several offers for train rides that users can compare directly on the SERP. Moreover,
the VSS unit is not displayed as prominently in terms of the size as the trains unit.
(360) Second, there is no reserved link to any other train travel VSS on the SERP as is the
case for the link to an extended version of the trains unit, which is included at the
bottom of the latter. The ‘More results’ link, which is displayed at the bottom of the
VSS unit, presents to the user results of various VSSs and, therefore, does not give
individual VSSs same prominence as the prominence given to Alphabet’s service via
the link reserved for it at the bottom of the trains unit.
(361) Third, the VSS tab does not compensate for the prominence given to Alphabet’s train
intermediation service through the ‘Trains’ tab. There are no tabs for individual
third-party VSSs displayed on top of the SERP, which would link to and show only the
offers and functionalities from their own inventory as is the case for Alphabet’s train

79
intermediation service via the ‘Trains’ tab. Given that the VSS tab shows the results of
various VSSs, it gives less prominence to individual third party VSSs compared to the
‘Trains’ tab, which exclusively shows the results of Alphabet’s own train
intermediation service.
(362) For the reasons stated above, the Commission concludes that Alphabet offers an
additional train intermediation service that is given more favourable treatment in
ranking on Google Search compared to similar services offered by third parties.
4.3.4.2. Alphabet’s arguments
(363) According to Alphabet, the Commission’s position that the trains unit is treated more
favourably in ranking than similar services offered by third parties on Google Search
is based on a flawed reasoning. To support this claim, Alphabet brings forward a
number of arguments. Arguments that do apply to train intermediation, but that do not
apply to flights intermediation or not in the same way, are included individually in the
remainder of this subsection. In all other cases, Alphabet brings forward the same
arguments as for the flights unit as set out in recitals (309) - (315) of this Decision.
4.3.4.2.1. Arguments about the March 2024 changes compensating for the prominence of
distinct Google services
(364) First, Alphabet’s arguments about having introduced multiple new designs for train
VSSs that created a disproportionate increase and visibility for VSSs are the same,
mutatis mutandis, as the arguments about new designs for flights VSSs set out in
recital (310) of this Decision, with the exception of the argument that it created a
counterbalance for the trains unit based on view and click data before and after 7
March 2024, since no such data was provided by Alphabet in the context of trains.
Second, Alphabet’s arguments about the Commission’s dismissal of the benefits to
VSSs from the March 2024 changes and its arguments regarding the Commission
overlooking VSS participation in the airlines unit are the same as for flights queries set
out in recitals (311) - (312) of this Decision.
4.3.4.2.2. Arguments about the lack of tangible advantage for distinct Google services
(365) Alphabets arguments are the same as those made in the context of flights queries set
out in recital (314) of this Decision.
4.3.4.2.3. Arguments about taking into account stakeholder interests
(366) Alphabets arguments are the same as those made in the context of flights queries set
out in recitals (316) - (317) of this Decision.
4.3.4.3. The Commission’s assessment of Alphabet’s arguments
(367) The Commission did not err in its analysis when establishing that the trains unit is
treated more favourably in ranking on Google Search compared to similar services
offered by third parties for the same reasons, mutatis mutandis, as for products and
flights queries, this is the case for the same reasons as set out in recitals (248) - (267)
and (316) - (317) of this Decision.

4.4.3. Third parties offer similar services which are ranked on the SERP
4.4.3.1. The Commission’s position
(400) Third parties offer services which have similar functionalities to those of Alphabet’s
lodging intermediation service that is ranked on and embedded in the SERP in
response to queries related to lodging. To the extent that they have a website, these
third-party lodging VSSs which intermediate hotels are ranked on the SERP in various
ways. This is because OSEs provide results based on search performed of in principles
all websites, absent any opt-out. Third-party offers may appear in the offer lists in the
preview page for a particular lodging offer if that hotel or other accommodation is
listed on those third-party websites as explained in recital (382) of this Decision.
(401) When a user submits a query on the website of such a third-party lodging VSS, they
are presented with a list of different hotels or other lodging offers matching the
location, number of guests and/or dates they entered. Typically, hotels and other
lodging offers are displayed with a picture, information about its location, price, rating
and ancillary information such as on the accommodation type and its amenities.
(402) Further, on their websites, third-party lodging VSS often do not only present their
hotel offers in the form of a list, but also as pins or small symbols, which may include
the hotel price, on a map. The map itself typically also displays street names,
landmarks, hospitals, and other relevant places in the area. Most maps on lodging VSS
websites are displayed together with filters, which narrow down the hotels shown on
the map based on the parameters selected. Similarly, a user can filter by location by
zooming in or out or dragging such a map.
(403) Clicking or sometimes hovering over any of the offers presented in the list of hotels or
on the corresponding map typically expands a ‘quick view’ card containing some

4.4.4. More favourable treatment in ranking on the SERP of Alphabet’s lodging
intermediation service
4.4.4.1. The Commission’s position
(413) When entering a lodging-related query, Alphabet’s lodging intermediation service is
given more favourable treatment in ranking on Google Search, as compared to
third-party lodging VSSs.
(414) Alphabet prominently embeds and ranks its own lodging intermediation service on
Google Search.
(415) First, Alphabet’s lodging unit is embedded on the SERP and can be seen by users
immediately after entering a lodging-related query. It consists of a large, dedicated box
displaying an interactive map as well as detailed information on short-term
accommodation offers by hotels or other lodging providers. This enables users, in the
lodging unit itself (i.e., directly on the SERP, immediately after entering a
lodging-related query), to search and compare several different lodging offers by
hotels with a view to initiating a transaction.
(416) Additionally, when clicking on any of the lodging offers in the list or on the map
included in the lodging unit, it is then presented with a preview page containing
further information about the hotel at issue, including, more images, information on
e.g., availability, prices, ratings, distance from relevant attractions, and ways to contact
the lodging provider. Also, the search results which are displayed following a click on
the ‘See more’ button (placed on the bottom of the lodging unit) or on the related
‘Lodging’ tab contain more lodging offers displaying the same type of
transaction-relevant information as the lodging unit.
(417) Third-party lodging VSSs also have opportunities to feature on the SERP. However,
they feature less prominently, as compared to Alphabet’s embedded lodging unit.
(418) First, third-party lodging VSSs may display offers in the lodging unit’s preview page,
which is only accessible once a user clicks on a specific hotel included in the lodging
unit or on the map of the lodging unit. However, for a third-party VSS this is not the
same as having its own box, embedded on the SERP and visible immediately after
entering a lodging-related query, containing several hotel offerings that users can
compare directly on the SERP, as is the case for Alphabet with its lodging unit.
(419) Second, a third-party VSS may also appear in free organic results, be it rich web
results or ordinary (i.e. non-rich) results.
(420) It is true that rich web results, which have an enhanced format, containing images as
well as information on the hotels at issue, also enable a third-party VSS to present

92
several hotel offerings in an embedded box. However, overall, the possibility for a
VSS to feature in rich web results does not compensate for the prominence given to
Alphabet’s lodging unit. This is because the prominence of the lodging unit is
strengthened by additional features which provide users with more possibilities to
compare accommodations with a view to initiate a transaction. In particular, as
described above, contrary to rich web results, the lodging unit is presented together
with a map, gives users access to a preview page with additional information and
includes a ‘See more’ button directing users to more lodging offers displaying the
same type of transaction-relevant information as in the unit, as does the ’Lodging’ tab
located on top of the SERP.
(421) Ordinary (i.e., non-rich) results, in turn, do not offer a third-party VSS a degree of
prominence comparable to that of Alphabet’s embedded lodging unit, as they do not
contain images or structured lodging-related information, and do not enable a VSS to
present different accommodation offerings that users can compare directly on the
SERP.
(422) Third, the possibility for a third-party VSS to feature in the VSS unit and in the
‘Places sites’ tab does not give it equal prominence as compared to Alphabet’s lodging
unit either.
(423) The VSS unit does not allow a given VSS to have its own box, embedded on the

(424) The possibility for a third-party VSS to include a link within the ‘Places sites’ tab is

4.5.3. Third parties offer similar services which are ranked on the SERP
4.5.3.1. The Commission’s position
(461) Third parties offer services, which have similar functionalities to those of Alphabet’s
local places intermediation service that is shown on the SERP in response to queries
related to local places. These third-party places VSSs are ranked on the SERP in
various ways. This is because OSEs provide results based on search performed of in
principles all websites, absent any opt-out.
(462) When a user submits a query on the website of such a third-party places VSS, they are
presented with a list of different places in the specific category matching their query.
For instance, when a user visits a third-party VSS’s website and searches for ‘Cafe
Brussels’, they are presented with a range of information including a photo of the café,
customer reviews, indicative pricing, the address, opening hours, phone number,
website, and other transactional details.
(463) Further, on their websites, third-party places VSSs often also present their offers as
small pins on a map. The map itself typically also displays street names, landmarks,
hospitals, and other relevant places in the area where the user is looking. Most maps
on places VSSs’ websites are displayed together with filters which narrow down the
places shown on the map based on the parameters entered. Similarly, zooming in or
out, or dragging such a map, functions as a filter for the locations in which the user
wants to look for a particular kind of place.
(464) Clicking or sometimes hovering over any of the offers presented in the list of places or
on the corresponding position on the map may also expand a ‘quick view’ card
containing some further ancillary information on that place such as a picture, its rating
by other users and the most relevant attributes such as the menu in case of restaurants.
(465) In addition, users can apply filters based on rating, price level, cuisine and other
parameters relevant for that particular kind of place and thereby refine their search on
the websites of third-party places VSSs. Some examples of similar third-party services
could be Yelp, TripAdvisor, TheFork, OpenTable or Foursquare city guide.
(466) As noted in recitals (436) - (442) of this Decision, the places unit displayed on the
SERP following a query related to local entities and its different features are similar to
the information and functionalities offered by third parties who provide places VSSs.
(467) Namely, as explained in recital (440) of this Decision, the places unit shows specific
information on local places offers in it in a list as well as on a map. Users can compare
places based on the transaction-relevant information provided to them directly on the
SERP. The type of information presented in the places unit is very similar to the
information displayed on the website of third-party places VSSs websites.
(468) Further, the preview page described in recital (441) of this Decision, that expands
when interacting with any of the places displayed as pins on the map or in the list of
offers below it in the places unit, is similar to the ‘quick view’ cards often included in
the list of places offers and the map on third-party places VSSs websites.
(469) For these reasons, the Commission concludes that third parties offer services, which
are ranked on Google Search, and which are similar to the additional places
intermediation service provided by Alphabet on the SERP.

(470) According to Alphabet, the Commission overlooks relevant differences between the

4.5.3.3. The Commission’s assessment of Alphabet’s arguments
(471) First, the Commission rejects Alphabet’s assertion that it ignored relevant differences

(472) Second, the Commission recalls that as set out in recital (206) of this Decision, the

4.5.4. More favourable treatment in ranking on the SERP of Alphabet’s places
intermediation service
4.5.4.1. The Commission’s position
(474) When entering a places-related query, Alphabet’s places intermediation service is
given more favourable treatment on Google Search, as compared to similar services
offered by third parties, in particular third-party places VSSs.
(475) Alphabet prominently embeds and ranks its own lodging intermediation service on
Google Search.
(476) First, Alphabet’s places unit is embedded on the SERP and can be seen by users
immediately after entering a places-related query. It consists of a large, dedicated unit
displaying an interactive map, as well as detailed information on restaurants,
attractions, or other offers related to the user’s places query from providers of local
places. This enables users, in the places unit itself (i.e., directly on the SERP,
immediately after entering a places-related query), to search and compare several
different places offers by local providers with a view to initiating a transaction.
Additionally, when clicking on any of the offers in the list or on the map included in
the places unit, a user is presented with a preview page containing further information
about the local entity at issue, including more images, information on e.g., availability,
price level, ratings, and ways to contact the local provider. Also, the search results
which are displayed following a click on the ‘See more’ button (placed on the bottom
of the places unit) or on the related ‘Places’ tab contain more places offers displaying
the same transaction-relevant information as the places unit.

(477) Third-party places VSSs also have opportunities to feature on the SERP. However,
they feature less prominently, as compared to Alphabet’s embedded places unit.
(478) First, third-party places VSSs cannot include their offers of the local places they
intermediate in the preview page that expands when a user clicks on that place in the
list or on the map of the places unit.254
(479) Second, third-party places VSSs’ may also appear in free organic results, be it rich
web results or ordinary (i.e. non-rich) results.
(480) It is true that rich web results, which have an enhanced format, containing images as
well as information on the places at issue, also enable a third-party VSS to present
several places offerings in an embedded box. However, overall, the possibility for a
VSS to feature in rich web results does not compensate for the prominence given to
Alphabet’s places unit. This is because the prominence of the places unit is
strengthened by additional features which provide users with more possibilities to
compare local places with a view to initiate a transaction. In particular, as described
above, contrary to rich web results, the places unit is presented together with a map,
gives users access to a preview page with additional information and includes a ‘See
more’ button directing users to more places offers displaying the same type of
transaction-relevant information as in the unit, as does the ’Places’ tab located on top
of the SERP.
(481) Ordinary (i.e., non-rich) results, in turn, do not offer a third-party VSS a degree of
prominence comparable to that of Alphabet’s embedded places unit, as they do not
contain images or structured place-related information, and do not enable a VSS to
present different places offerings that users can compare directly on the SERP.
(482) Third, the possibility for a third-party VSS to feature in the VSS unit and in the
‘Places sites’ tab does not give it equal prominence as compared to Alphabet’s places
unit either.
(483) The VSS unit does not allow a given VSS to have its own box, embedded on the
SERP and visible immediately after entering a places-related query, containing several
places offerings that users can compare directly on the SERP.
(484) The possibility for a third-party VSS to include a link within the ‘Places sites’ tab is
not the same as it having its own box, embedded on the SERP and visible immediately
after entering a places-related query, containing several local places offerings that
users can compare directly on the SERP. Additionally, it is noteworthy that, while
there are no tabs for individual third-party places VSSs displayed on top of the SERP,
which would link to and show only the offers from their respective inventory, the
results in the ‘Places’ tab are an extended version of those displayed in Alphabet’s
places unit. Given that the ‘Places sites’ tab shows the results of various VSSs, it gives
less prominence to individual third-party VSSs compared to the ‘Places’ tab, which
exclusively shows results of Alphabet’s places unit.

4.6.2. Google Maps is distinct from Google Search and is ranked on the SERP
(493) Google Maps is an online-based consumer map service which enables users to search
for and navigate to local entities,256 including local businesses and has been designated
as an OIS in the Alphabet designation decision, which has not been contested by
Alphabet.257 Because Google Maps falls into a different category of CPS than OSE
Google Search, and because it has been designated as such, it is distinct from Google
Search.
(494) In response to the Commission’s RFI, Alphabet brought forward arguments contesting
that it offers distinct services on the SERP, including the linking out to Google Maps
in the preview page.
(495) Alphabet argues that the ‘directions’ and ‘address’ buttons are elements of the result
for a local entity such as a hotel or place, that provides an alternative to a website link
to find and reach the relevant entity. Alphabet also argues that by showing directions
or address links as part of a result for a local entity, Google Search is not ranking a
separate result. Rather it is interoperating with Google Maps to connect users with
local entities in the real world which is not governed by Article 6(5) but by Article
6(7) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925.258
(496) The Commission considers that Alphabet’s distinction between separate search results
and elements of search results is irreconcilable with the wording of Regulation (EU)
2022/1925. Article 2, point (23), of that Regulation defines ‘search results’ broadly as
including “any product, service or information offered in connection with the organic
results”. By providing links to Google Maps, Google Search offers a distinct service in
connection with organic results.
(497) In line with the broad notion of ‘search results’, contrary to Alphabet’s claim, buttons
linking to Google Maps are subject to Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 if
they are ranked on the OSE of the same gatekeeper.
(498) The Commission notes that linking to a distinct service and thereby ranking it on the
SERP is not synonymous with ensuring interoperability by means of mutual exchange
of information between software as evident from the different definitions in Article 2,
points (22) and (29) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925.
(499) For these reasons, the Commission considers that Alphabet offers Google Maps, a
distinct service which is ranked on and embedded in the SERP.

(523) The translation unit displayed by Alphabet on the SERP constitutes a content-related

(524) First, with the translation unit, which is ranked on and embedded in Google Search,
Alphabet provides a distinct or additional translation service to the user on the SERP.
The service provided in the translation unit has a purpose that is different from or
goes beyond that of an OSE, in terms of the functionalities or tasks that it performs.
(525) In particular, the translation unit presents a series of functionalities and performs
tasks that allow users to perform, directly on the SERP, actions that go beyond
searching the Internet and obtaining results in which information related to the
requested content can be found. Indeed, it enables a user not only to see the results of

(542) In the first place, while it is true that the translation unit provides direct answers to

(543) In the second place, as regards Alphabet’s argument that the translation unit does not

that Alphabet’s own translation services have more prominence on the SERP,
compared to third-party services, has resulted in an advantage for the former and a
disadvantage for the latter. However, the Commission is under no duty to investigate
the possible impact, effect, or harm deriving from non-compliance with Article 6(5)

Regulation that the assessment to be carried out by the Commission is independent
“from the actual, potential or presumed effects of the conduct of a given gatekeeper
covered by this Regulation on competition on a given market”.
5.1.7. Conclusion
(552) For the reasons stated above, the Commission concludes that Alphabet gives its own
translation services, in particular its translation unit and ‘Google Translate’, more
favourable treatment in ranking on Google Search, as compared to similar services
offered by third parties.

(582) The games unit displayed by Alphabet on the SERP constitutes a content-related
service that is distinct or additional to Google Search.
(583) First, with the games unit, which is ranked on and embedded in Google Search,
Alphabet provides a distinct or additional games service to the user on the SERP. The
service provided in the games unit has a purpose that is different from or goes
beyond that of an OSE, in terms of the functionalities or tasks that it performs.
(584) In particular, the games unit presents a series of functionalities that allow users to
perform, directly on the SERP, actions that are unrelated to searching the Internet and
obtaining results in which information related to the requested content can be found.
Indeed, it enables a user not only to see the results of a games-related search query
that it has previously submitted, but also to play such a game directly on the SERP, in
an ad hoc interactive rectangle box that has been specifically designed for these
purposes.
(585) Second, Alphabet does not offer the games displayed in the games unit by sourcing
data from any websites (whether, for instance, by crawling or through data-feeds),

as required under the definition of an OSE provided in Article 2, point (6), of
Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 by reference to Article 2, point (5), of Regulation (EU)
2019/1150. This provides additional evidence that such a unit constitutes a service
that is distinct or additional to Google Search.

SERP constitutes a service that is distinct or additional to Google Search.

(587) A wide range of third-party websites offer games services that are similar to those

crazygames.com. Virtually all these third-party websites are, or are likely to be,
indexed by Google Search and consequently ranked on the SERP, in response to
certain queries.

its games unit, are given more favourable treatment in ranking on Google Search, as
compared to similar services offered by third parties.

5.3.6. The Commission’s assessment of Alphabet’s arguments
(596) First, Alphabet has not put forward any convincing arguments calling into question
the Commission’s conclusion that the games unit displayed by Alphabet on the SERP
constitutes a service that is distinct or additional to Google Search.
(597) In the first place, whether the games unit may be characterized as an ‘ancillary’
feature is not decisive. Indeed, the question whether the games unit constitutes a
service that is distinct or additional to Google Search depends, in particular, on
whether it has a different purpose from that of an OSE, and not on its possible
‘ancillary’ or ‘non-ancillary’ nature. And the fact remains that the purpose of the
games unit is different from or goes beyond that of an OSE, as, rather than searching
the Internet and delivering to users results in which information related to the
requested content can be found, it enables users to play games directly on the SERP.
(598) In the second place, while it may be true that other products or services may include
the same type of games as those displayed in the games unit, Alphabet has not
argued, let alone demonstrated, that the entities providing such products or services
have been designated as gatekeepers under Regulation (EU) 2022/1925, that such
products or services constitute core platform services listed in a designation decision
pursuant to Article 3(9) of that Regulation, or that such products or services engage
in ‘ranking’, which is a necessary precondition for the application of Article 6(5) of
Regulation (EU) 2022/1925. Additionally, Alphabet has not explained whether or to
what extent such games fall within the purpose of those products or services, or, if
that were to be the case, why that would mean that they also fall within the purpose
of an OSE.
(599) In the third place, the fact that only a small percentage of queries issued in the EEA
result in the display of a games unit, supposing it were established, would not call
into question the Commission’s findings set out in recitals (582) - (586) of this
Decision. Indeed, what is important to determine whether there is a distinct or
additional service is, in particular, the purpose of such service, not the frequency with
which it is displayed.
(600) Second, Alphabet has not put forward any convincing arguments calling into
question the Commission’s conclusion that Alphabet’s own games services, in
particular its games unit, are given more favourable treatment in ranking on Google
Search, as compared to similar services offered by third parties, mutatis mutandis, for
the reasons set out in recitals (550) and (551) of this Decision.
5.3.7. Conclusion
(601) For the reasons stated above, the Commission concludes that Alphabet gives its own
games services, in particular its games unit, more favourable treatment in ranking on
Google Search, as compared to similar services offered by third parties.
6. ALPHABET’S ALLEGATIONS REGARDING PROCEDURAL DEFICIENCIES ARE UNFOUNDED
(602) Alphabet alleges that the Commission’s investigation suffers from procedural errors.
Alphabet raises three main arguments:

125
● The scope of the investigation is larger than what was set out in the Opening
Decision.
● The investigation was in breach of the principle of sound administration.
● Alphabet’s rights of defence were breached because it did not have proper
access to file.
(603) Alphabet’s claims are unfounded. The Commission’s investigation was fully in scope
of the Opening Decision, conducted in line with the principle of sound
administration and in full respect of Alphabet’s rights of defence.
6.1. Scope of the Commission’s investigation
6.1.1. Alphabet’s arguments about large portions of the Preliminary Findings being
outside the scope of the Commission’s investigation
(604) Alphabet claims that the Commission’s investigation is broader than the scope of the
Opening Decision, in breach of Article 5 of Commission Implementing Regulation
(EU) 2023/814, according to which the Preliminary Findings can only be adopted
based on the Opening Decision.303
(605) First, as regards transactional queries, Alphabet claims that the Commission’s
investigation should be limited to the assessment of the compliance with Article 6(5)
Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 of the elements listed in paragraph 8 of the Opening
Decision.304 Therefore, according to Alphabet, the free units for suppliers should be
excluded of such assessment given that only the preview pages, query shortcut chips
and tabs are in scope of the present case. Additionally Alphabet claims that trains
and airlines units do not include a preview page and the tabs for trains, airlines and
products are the only ones in scope.305
(606) Second, as regards the units displayed in response to a content query, such as sports,
Alphabet considers them to be “entirely unrelated to the matters identified in the
opening decision”.306
6.1.2. The Commission’s assessment of Alphabet’s arguments
(607) First, the Commission fully complied with its procedural obligations under
Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 and Commission Implementing Regulation (EU)
2023/814.
(608) Pursuant to Article 20 of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 the Commission adopted an
opening decision on 25 March 2024 with a view to the possible adoption of a
decision pursuant to Article 29 of that Regulation. Article 20 Regulation (EU)
2022/1925 does not specify the content of such an opening decision. Article 29(3) of
that Regulation requires the Commission to communicate preliminary findings to the

(609) The Opening Decision therefore does not limit the Commission’s ability to determine

procedural step which serves to inform the parties that the Commission will further
investigate a specific conduct. Pursuant to Article 34 Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 the
Commission shall base its decision on its preliminary findings, and not the opening
decision. Additionally, an opening decision serves to inform the national competition
authorities and national courts of Members States that the Commission is conducting
an investigation on the matter.
(610) Thus, Alphabets errs in stating that the Commission could not include additional
facts and legal arguments after the Opening Decision.
(611) Second, in any event, the Opening Decision had a broad scope which referred not

but more broadly to Alphabet’s services compliance with Article 6(5) Regulation

(612) Recital 8 of the Opening Decision outlined the measures that Alphabet took to

● The compliance of those measures with Alphabet’s obligation to not

● whether those measures undermined effective compliance as they did not fully

(613) Recital 10 of that Decision concludes that the investigation will focus on “the
