7. DURATION OF ALPHABET’S NON-COMPLIANCE
(641) The Commission finds that Alphabet’s non-compliance with Article 6(5) of
Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 commenced on the date when that provision became
applicable to it, that is on 7 March 2024, which is six months after the online search
engine Google Search was listed in the Alphabet designation decision. This
non-compliance is still ongoing at the date of adoption of this Decision.
8. ADDRESSEES
(642) The Commission concludes that the infringement of Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU)
2022/1925 should be imputed to Alphabet Inc., since it was (i) the addressee of the
decision designating Alphabet as a gatekeeper pursuant to Article 3 of Regulation
(EU) 2022/1925; (ii) the legal entity which – for the entire period of the infringement
– formulated and rolled out features and functionalities on the Google SERP which are
the subject of this Decision; (iii) the legal entity which (directly or indirectly) wholly
owned and continues to fully own Google Ireland Ltd., which is the legal entity that
operates the Alphabet’s OSE CPS Google Search and further services concerned by
this Decision in the Union.335
9. FINES
9.1. Principles
(643) Under Article 30(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925, the Commission may by
decision impose fines on gatekeepers where it finds that the gatekeeper, intentionally
or negligently, fails to comply with any of the obligations laid down in Articles 5, 6,
and 7 of that Regulation. Fines under Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 are aimed at
ensuring effective compliance by the gatekeepers with their obligations under
applicable laws and prevention of non-compliant conduct that could undermine the
objectives of applicable law (i.e., in the present case Regulation (EU) 2022/1925).

(644) According to Article 30(4) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925, in fixing the amount of a

(645) Any fine imposed by the Commission shall not exceed 10 % of the gatekeeper’s total
worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year. Additionally, the Commission

proportionality,337 while having, at the same time, the necessary deterrent effect.338
9.2. Intent or negligence
(646) As mentioned in recital (643) of this Decision, a fine may be imposed on gatekeepers
that ‘intentionally or negligently’ fail to comply with any of the obligations laid
down in Articles 5, 6, and 7 of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925.
9.2.1. The Commission’s position
(647) The Commission finds that Alphabet acted at the very least negligently, as it could
not have been unaware339 that the conduct described in Sections 4 and 5 of this
Decision did not comply with Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925.
(648) First, Alphabet could not have been unaware that such conduct could lead to a breach
of Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 given the clear language of Article
6(5) and recitals 51 and 52 of that Regulation, as well as the stated objectives
thereof. In particular, the conditions to ensure compliance with Article 6(5) of
Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 are clearly set out in that provision, according to which
the gatekeeper shall not treat more favourably, in ranking and related indexing and
crawling, services and products offered by the gatekeeper itself than similar services
or products of a third party.
(649) Additionally, recital 51 of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 clarifies, in essence, that
non-compliance with Article 6(5) of that Regulation can occur, for instance, in
relation to products or services, including other core platform services, which are
ranked in the results communicated by online search engines, or which are partly or
entirely embedded in online search engines results, groups of results specialised in a
certain topic, displayed along with the results of an online search engine, which are
considered or used by certain users as a service distinct or additional to the online
search engine.

9.3. Calculation of the fine
9.3.1. Gravity
9.3.1.1. The Commission’s position
(669) Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 lists the gravity of the non-compliance as one of the key
criteria to determine the level of the fine for non-compliance. In the present case, the
Commission concludes that several factors are relevant to assess the gravity of
Alphabet’s non-compliance with Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 in
relation to Google Search.
(670) First, Alphabet’s non-compliance with Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925
concerns users in all Member States and thus covers the whole of the Union.
(671) Second, Alphabet’s non-compliance with Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925
affects a large number of users established or located in the Union. Indeed, as
established in the Alphabet designation decision, according to data provided by
Alphabet itself, the Google Search CPS had a large number of monthly active end
users established or located in the Union in 2022 ([300-400 million] signed-in
accounts and [400-500 million] signed-out cookie counts).359 Relevant third-party
offers and content are presented to these users with less prominence as a result of
Alphabet’s non-compliant conduct.
(672) Alphabet’s non-compliance with Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 also
affects a large number of businesses established in the Union, in particular VSSs and
direct suppliers. Indeed, as established in the Alphabet designation decision,
according to data provided by Alphabet itself, the Google Search CPS had
approximately [5-10 billion] yearly active business users established in the Union in
2022.360 Offers and content provided by a number of businesses are ranked less
prominently on the SERP as compared to Alphabet’s own services.
(673) Third, the Commission considers that Alphabet has violated Article 6(5) of
Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 through a number of conducts, described in Sections 4
and 5 of this Decision. Indeed, Alphabet has treated a significant number of its own
services more favourably in ranking as compared to similar third-party services,
including both services related to transactional queries (in particular, products, flights
trains, lodging and places intermediation services, as well as Google Maps), and

services related to content queries (in particular, sport information, translation, and
games services).
(674) Fourth, when assessing the gravity of Alphabet’s non-compliance with Article 6(5)
of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925, the Commission must ensure that fines have a
sufficiently deterrent effect in relation to Alphabet, but also in relation to other
designated gatekeepers to avoid future breaches of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925. In
that regard, the link between, on the one hand, the undertaking’s size and global
resources and, on the other, the need to ensure that a fine has a deterrent effect cannot
be denied. Accordingly, when the Commission calculates the amount of the fine it
may take into consideration, inter alia, the size and the economic power of the
undertaking concerned.361
(675) Alphabet is one of the largest technology companies in the world by turnover.
Alphabet’s total worldwide turnover in the business year ending 31 December 2025
was USD 402 836 000 000 (approximately EUR 356 509 860 000).362 Alphabet had
an estimated market capitalisation of approximately USD 3 672 000 000 000 on 20
February 2026 (approximately EUR 3 124 137 600 000),363 making it the third most
valuable company in the world in terms of market capitalisation on that date.364 As a
result, Alphabet can be regarded as a very large company with significant economic
power and resources, including legal resources.
(676) In light of the above, the gravity of Alphabet’s non-compliance with Article 6(5) of
Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 should be considered as serious.

9.3.1.3. The Commission’s assessment of Alphabet’s arguments
(680) First, the Commission is under no duty to investigate the possible impact, effect, or

that the assessment to be carried out by the Commission is independent “from the
actual, potential or presumed effects of the conduct of a given gatekeeper covered by
this Regulation on competition on a given market”.
(681) In any event, as demonstrated in this Decision, the conduct described in Sections 4
and 5 of this Decision, put in place by Alphabet in March 2024, provided more
prominence on Google Search to Alphabet’s own services compared to similar
third-party services. This may, in itself, be considered to adversely affect, in
particular, any third parties whose services would have benefited from more
prominence in terms of presentation had Alphabet complied with Article 6(5) of
Regulation (EU) 2022/1925.

such non-compliance impacted a significant number of businesses and users
throughout the entire Union, across a wide range of services related to transactional
and content-related queries (see recitals (670) - (673) of this Decision).

calling into question the serious gravity of the non-compliance.

including those pursuant to Article 6(5) thereof, began to apply to Alphabet.

approximately 28 months.

(688) The Commission considers that there are no aggravating circumstances in this case.

9.3.4.2.1. The Commission’s position
(689) The Commission concludes that there is a mitigating circumstance in this case.

designation of gatekeepers and the obligations applicable to them.369 This Decision is
also among the very first non-compliance decisions under Regulation (EU)

(690) Alphabet argues that the Commission should take into account four mitigating

(691) First, Alphabet contends that it has engaged with the Commission in good faith, and

(692) Second, Alphabet alleges that the Commission has not identified any tangible
evidence of consumer harm.
(693) Third, Alphabet maintains that the state of the law is unclear and that the problems

are complex.

this did not go beyond its obligation stemming from the duty to cooperate in a
non-compliance investigation. Additionally, the Commission notes that, despite such
interactions, Alphabet’s non-compliance with Article 6(5) Regulation (EU)
2022/1925 remains ongoing.
(695) This conclusion is not called into question by Alphabet’s reference, by analogy, to
paragraph 29, fourth bullet, of the Commission’s Guidelines on the method of setting

recognizes, as a mitigating circumstance, the fact that an undertaking has effectively

beyond its legal obligation to do so. Indeed, these guidelines refer to competition law
infringements, not to non-compliance with Regulation (EU) 2022/1925, and
Alphabet has not explained why they are relevant in the present context. Even if they
were, Alphabet has not explained why, in its view, it has cooperated with the
Commission beyond its legal obligation to do so, within the meaning of those
guidelines. Additionally, and in any event, according to the case-law of the EU
Courts, this mitigating circumstance can only be accepted exceptionally, in particular
when an undertaking’s cooperation facilitates the Commission’s task of finding and
bringing competition law infringements to an end.371 No such exceptional
circumstances exist in the present case.

duty to investigate the possible impact, effect, or harm deriving from non-compliance

warrant a reduction of the fine. Additionally, while Alphabet argues that it has sought

9.3.5. Conclusion
(699) In view of the above, the Commission considers that Alphabet has, at the very least
negligently, not complied with Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925.
Alphabet’s non-compliance with that provision is serious as it covered the entirety of
the Union, affected a large number of businesses and users in the Union, and
involved a number of different non-compliant conducts. Furthermore, Alphabet is a
large undertaking, with substantial resources, including legal resources. Alphabet’s
non-compliance is of medium duration. Finally, the Commission has taken into
account the mitigating circumstance that this Decision is among the very first
non-compliance decisions adopted under Regulation (EU) 2022/1925, and
specifically Article 6(5) thereof.
9.4. Amount of the fine
(700) In view of the criteria described in recitals (646) - (699) of this Decision, the
Commission considers it appropriate to impose a fine under Article 30(1)(a) of
Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 representing EUR 460 000 000.
(701) As explained in recital (675) of this Decision, Alphabet’s total worldwide turnover in
the business year ending 31 December 2025 was USD 402 836 000 000
(approximately EUR 356 509 860 000). The final amount of the fine set is thus
below 10 % of that figure, which is the maximum fine that could be imposed
pursuant to Article 30(1) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925.
(702) This amount is proportionate, as it represents a relatively small proportion of
Alphabet’s annual worldwide turnover (approximately 0.13 %) and in any event
significantly less than the maximum fine cap of 10 % referred to in recital (701) of
this Decision.
9.5. Right to be heard and principle of sound administration with respect to the fine
(703) Alphabet argues, in essence, that imposing a fine on it in the present case would
breach its right to be heard, its rights of defence, and the principle of sound
administration because the Commission’s Preliminary Findings merely referred to
the fining criteria established in Article 30(4) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925, without
however providing any information on how the Commission would apply such
criteria and calculate the fine.372
(704) In this regard, first, contrary to what Alphabet maintains, the Preliminary Findings
did not limit themselves to stating that the fine would consider the gravity, duration,
and recurrence of the non-compliance. Indeed, in recitals (345) - (351) of the
Preliminary Findings, the Commission explained the different elements that it would
take into account in assessing each of these three criteria, such as, for the assessment
of gravity, notably the geographic scope and the number of users affected by the
non-compliance. The Commission added, in particular, that it would consider any
aggravating or mitigating circumstances, as well as the need to ensure sufficient
deterrence bearing in mind Alphabet’s size and financial capacity.

decision, the Commission shall order the gatekeeper to cease and desist with the
non-compliance within an appropriate deadline and to provide explanations on how it
plans to comply with that decision”.

Alphabet to bring the non-compliance described in Sections 4 and 5 of this Decision
effectively to an end within 60 calendar days from the date of notification of this
Decision (the ‘Cease and Desist Order’).
(709) In addition, it is necessary to ensure that Alphabet shall refrain from repeating any
conduct constituting non-compliance with Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925,
as well as from any conduct having the same or equivalent object or effect.

similar services offered by third parties, as explained in recitals (519) - (601) of
this Decision. First, this is due to the fact that certain services have a purpose
that is different to or goes beyond the purpose of an OSE in terms of the
functionalities that they have and the tasks that they perform. In particular,
Alphabet displays groups of results or dedicated units, specialised in a certain
topic, with specific functionalities that, individually or in combination, allow
users to perform actions directly on the SERP that are unrelated to or otherwise
go beyond searching the Internet and obtaining results in which information
related to the requested content can be found. Second, this is due to the fact that

147
certain services are not assembled by performing searches of, in principle, all
websites;
(c) Displaying interactive pointers to its own distinct or additional services on the
Google SERP, such as in tabs or in links to these services when a user clicks on
a reservations, directions or any other button on the Google SERP with more
prominence than similar services offered by third parties, as set out in recitals
(490) - (517) of this Decision.
(713) It is for Alphabet to identify and implement the measures to ensure compliance with
Article 6(5) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925. One end of the range of possibilities to
do so, in particular, is that Alphabet can extend the prominence it gives to its own
distinct or additional services as set out in recital (712) of this Decision equally to
similar services offered by third parties. On the other end, Alphabet may remove all
prominence it affords its own distinct or additional services as set out in recital (712)
of this Decision.
(714) In addition to terminating the non-compliance identified in Sections 4 and 5 of this
Decision, Alphabet should implement measures that prevent the recurrence of
non-compliance. When submitting its proposed measures, Alphabet should ensure
that its proposal is sufficiently reasoned and detailed to enable the Commission to
assess whether the proposed measures will ensure that the non-compliance has been
terminated and the recurrence of the non-compliance is avoided and thus that it will
be effectively brought to an end.
11. PERIODIC PENALTY PAYMENTS
11.1. The Commission’s position
(715) In view of the seriousness of Alphabet’s non-compliance with Article 6(5) of
Regulation (EU) 2022/1925, as established in this Decision, and considering that the
non-compliance has been found to be ongoing, the Commission concludes that it is
necessary to impose periodic penalty payments pursuant to Article 31(1), point (h),
of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925, in case Alphabet were to fail to implement measures
that bring the non-compliance effectively to an end within 60 calendar days from the
date of notification of this Decision.
(716) Any periodic penalty payments that may be definitively set should be sufficient to
ensure compliance by Alphabet with this Decision and may take account of
Alphabet’s significant financial resources (see recitals (674) and (675) of this
Decision).
11.2. Alphabet’s arguments
(717) Alphabet argues, in essence, that imposing periodic penalty payments in the present
case is unwarranted, let alone imposing the maximum amount thereof.375

(718) First, Alphabet contends that, in the Preliminary Findings, the Commission did not
provide any reasoning for imposing the maximum amount of periodic penalty
payments.376
(719) Second, Alphabet claims that imposing the maximum amount of periodic penalty

(720) Third, Alphabet alleges that imposing the maximum amount of periodic penalty
payments is only appropriate in ‘the most egregious cases’, when a gatekeeper
refuses to comply in any way whatsoever with an obligation.378
(721) Fourth, Alphabet maintains that when imposing periodic penalty payments in the
present case, the Commission should take into account the mitigating factors set out
in recitals (691) - (693) of this Decision.379
11.3. The Commission’s assessment of Alphabet’s arguments
(722) First, contrary to what Alphabet maintains, the Commission did provide sufficient
reasoning on the imposition of periodic penalty payments in the Preliminary
Findings. Indeed, in recital (353) of the Preliminary Findings, the Commission
justified the imposition of periodic penalty payments, as well as the level thereof, in
view of the seriousness of Alphabet’s non-compliance and referred to the recitals of
the Preliminary Findings regarding the gravity of Alphabet’s non-compliance.
(723) Second, as regards the three Commission precedents mentioned by Alphabet, namely
the Commission decisions in Microsoft,380 Apple (Art. 5(4)),381 and Meta (Art.
5(2)),382 it must be noted that, according to the case-law of the EU Courts, the
Commission is required to carry out an individual appraisal of the circumstances of
each case, without being bound by previous decisions concerning other undertakings
or other CPSs.383 Additionally, Alphabet has not demonstrated that the circumstances
in those cases were comparable to those in the present case. In any event, the
Commission’s approach in the present case, with regard to periodic penalty
payments, is, in essence, the same as that followed in the Apple (Art. 5(4)) and Meta
(Art. 5(2)) cases.
(724) Third, Alphabet’s argument that imposing the maximum amount of periodic penalty
payments is only appropriate when a gatekeeper refuses to comply in any way
whatsoever with an obligation must be rejected. Indeed, according to the case-law of
the EU Courts, a number of factors may be taken into account when imposing and

(725) In the present case, while it is true that Alphabet’s March 2024 measures were
implemented in connection with Alphabet’s efforts to comply with Regulation (EU)
2022/1925, the fact remains that, despite clear indications from the Commission that
such measures did not comply with Article 6(5) of that Regulation, Alphabet did not
make any further changes to such measures and its non-compliance is still ongoing at

Decision, the gravity of Alphabet’s non-compliance in the present case must be
considered as serious, and it is important to ensure deterrence, bearing in mind that
Alphabet is one of the largest technology companies in the world.
(726) Fourth, Alphabet’s argument that the Commission should take into account the
mitigating circumstances set out in recitals (691) - (693) of this Decision must be
rejected for the reasons set out in recitals (694) - (698) of this Decision.
(727) It follows from the above that Alphabet has not put forward any convincing
arguments against the imposition of periodic penalty payments by the Commission.
